one_line: Foundation models place medical boundaries at intensity gradients even when clinical ground truth is defined functionally, producing a measurable systematic offset.
problem: Many clinical boundaries (tumor margins with microscopic infiltration, edema halos) are defined by treatment convention rather than by a visible edge, yet promptable foundation models were pretrained on natural images where object boundaries coincide with photometric edges.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model boundary placement in medical images is an edge-snapping process: predicted contours are attracted to the locally strongest intensity gradient regardless of the task definition of the target boundary.
falsifiable_prediction: Across structures whose ground-truth contour is deliberately offset from the strongest gradient (e.g., clinical target volumes with fixed margins), the signed distance from predicted contour to the nearest strong gradient will be significantly smaller than the signed distance to the ground-truth contour, and this bias will persist after fine-tuning with limited data.
why_important: If boundary error is a systematic edge-snapping bias rather than random noise, averaging, ensembling, and more data will not fix it; margin-critical applications like radiotherapy planning would need a structurally different decoding objective.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary error is usually reported as an aggregate surface distance; decomposing it into gradient-attraction bias versus residual noise as an explicit, testable mechanism appears less explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one public dataset where the labeled boundary is convention-defined rather than edge-defined, compute for each boundary point the offset between prediction, label, and nearest strong gradient, and test whether the prediction-to-gradient distance distribution is tighter than prediction-to-label.
main_risk: Suitable public datasets with convention-defined boundaries and reliable labels may be scarce, and gradient strength must be defined carefully to avoid a circular measure.
default_community_belief: Boundary errors of foundation models are treated as generic imprecision that scales down with more medical fine-tuning data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuned models may learn convention offsets easily because the offset is locally constant, making the bias disappear after even modest adaptation.
fastest_falsification: A one-day analysis on an existing model's predictions: histogram of contour-to-gradient versus contour-to-label distances on any margin-convention dataset.

one_line: Where human raters disagree most, single-mask foundation models are most confidently wrong rather than uncertain.
problem: Inter-rater variability defines an irreducible ambiguity zone in medical segmentation, but foundation models output a single deterministic mask with high confidence everywhere.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model confidence is anti-correlated with rater consensus in ambiguity zones: the model commits to one plausible contour mode with high logit confidence exactly where raters spread out.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-rater datasets, voxelwise model confidence inside the inter-rater disagreement band will not be significantly lower than confidence in consensus regions at matched distance-to-boundary, contradicting the assumption that confidence tracks ambiguity.
why_important: Clinical deployment plans often use model confidence for triage; if confidence is blind to genuine ambiguity, triage will systematically miss the cases that most need human review.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration studies usually compare confidence to a single ground truth; conditioning the analysis on rater-disagreement maps as the ambiguity reference is a different question.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use any public multi-rater segmentation dataset, compute rater-disagreement maps, stratify model confidence by disagreement level while controlling for distance to the mean contour, and test for the predicted flat or inverted relationship.
main_risk: Distance-to-boundary is a strong confounder; without careful matching the analysis can rediscover the trivial fact that boundaries are uncertain.
default_community_belief: Softmax or mask-logit confidence of large pretrained models is assumed to be a usable proxy for ambiguity after simple recalibration.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary-adjacent confidence dips may already capture most rater disagreement because raters mostly disagree near boundaries anyway.
fastest_falsification: Correlation analysis between existing model entropy maps and published rater-variance maps on one dataset; requires no training.

one_line: Single-mask decoders collapse multimodal contour distributions to one rater style rather than an average, and which mode wins is dataset-order dependent.
problem: When training labels mix several annotation conventions, a deterministic segmentation head must resolve the conflict somehow, and how foundation models resolve it is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Fine-tuned foundation models do not average conflicting conventions; they lock onto the convention of whichever subset dominates early training batches, making the learned boundary style an artifact of data ordering.
falsifiable_prediction: Two fine-tuning runs differing only in data order, on a corpus with two labeled conventions, will produce models whose contours match different conventions, with between-run contour disagreement concentrated in the inter-convention band.
why_important: Multi-institutional training is the default path to scale; if convention capture is order-dependent, reported model behavior is unreproducible in a clinically meaningful way.
why_possibly_novel: Run-to-run variance is usually measured as Dice noise; attributing it to discrete convention capture with a designed two-convention corpus is a sharper claim.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a mixed corpus by relabeling one structure under two explicit rules (e.g., include versus exclude a visible capsule), fine-tune twice with different seeds and orders, and measure which rule each model reproduces.
main_risk: The effect may require label conflicts larger than those in realistic corpora, making the demonstration artificial.
default_community_belief: Training on mixed conventions yields a stable averaged boundary, and seed variance is negligible noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SGD may genuinely interpolate conventions at the voxel level because the loss is convex in the output probabilities for fixed features.
fastest_falsification: Two small fine-tuning runs on a synthetically bi-conventional dataset and a paired contour comparison.

one_line: Predicted contour curvature statistics of foundation models match natural-image object statistics, not anatomical shape statistics.
problem: Anatomy has characteristic curvature spectra (smooth organ capsules, high-curvature folds); pretraining on natural images may impose a wrong prior on contour geometry.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model masks carry a transferable curvature prior from pretraining: their contour curvature spectrum deviates from ground-truth anatomy toward the curvature spectrum of natural-image objects, especially in low-contrast regions where the prior dominates the likelihood.
falsifiable_prediction: The distribution of local contour curvature of zero-shot predictions will differ from ground truth in a consistent direction across organs, and the deviation will grow as local image contrast decreases.
why_important: A geometric prior mismatch predicts where models fail without needing labels, enabling targeted review; it also suggests that shape-aware decoding, not more data, is the fix.
why_possibly_novel: Failure analyses focus on overlap metrics; treating curvature spectra as a fingerprint of the pretraining prior is an unusual measurement.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute curvature histograms for predicted versus ground-truth contours on one CT and one MR dataset, stratified by local contrast, and test for a consistent directional shift.
main_risk: Curvature estimation on voxelized masks is noisy and resolution-dependent; the effect could be an artifact of mask discretization.
default_community_belief: Pretraining priors are assumed to transfer only as generic edge and texture features, not as measurable shape-statistics biases in outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decoder upsampling and post-processing may dominate contour geometry, erasing any pretraining shape prior.
fastest_falsification: Curvature-spectrum comparison on existing zero-shot predictions; purely analytical, no training.

one_line: Prompt-perturbation instability is a label-free probe that localizes clinically ambiguous boundary regions.
problem: Identifying which boundary segments are ambiguous normally requires multiple raters, which is expensive; a cheap intrinsic probe would be valuable.
core_hypothesis: For promptable models, the local flip rate of mask boundaries under small prompt perturbations is causally linked to image-intrinsic ambiguity and therefore predicts inter-rater disagreement zones without any labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Voxelwise prompt-jitter flip maps will correlate with multi-rater disagreement maps substantially better than image-gradient baselines and better than model entropy at matched compute.
why_important: A validated label-free ambiguity probe would let institutions target their scarce multi-rater annotation budget and would give deployment-time review maps.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is usually treated as a robustness defect to minimize; reinterpreting it as an ambiguity sensor with quantitative validation against raters inverts the framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, generate flip maps from N jittered prompts per case, compute correlation with rater disagreement, and compare against entropy and gradient baselines.
main_risk: Flip maps may mostly reflect model-specific artifacts (patch grid, prompt encoding) rather than image ambiguity.
default_community_belief: Prompt sensitivity is noise to be engineered away, and ambiguity estimation requires ensembles or explicit probabilistic heads.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rater disagreement includes protocol and style components invisible to any image-based probe, capping the achievable correlation at a low value.
fastest_falsification: One inference-only experiment on an existing multi-rater dataset with an off-the-shelf promptable model.

one_line: Foundation models systematically truncate structures at partial-volume ends, and the truncation length is predictable from the point spread function.
problem: Thin structure tips and organ poles fade gradually due to partial-volume averaging; how learned models decide where a structure ends in fading signal is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Foundation models apply an implicit intensity threshold learned from pretraining statistics, so they truncate fading structures at a fixed fraction of peak contrast, making the missed length a deterministic function of local PSF and contrast rather than random error.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic phantoms with controlled PSF blur, the length of missed structure tip will scale linearly with blur width at fixed contrast, with a slope stable across structure types, and real-data tip errors will match the phantom-derived slope.
why_important: Tip truncation drives clinically important errors (vessel length, lesion extent); a predictable law would allow analytic correction instead of retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Connecting dense-prediction failure quantitatively to acquisition PSF via phantoms, and validating the same constant on real data, treats the model as a measurable instrument.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate blurred synthetic tubes and cones spanning blur and contrast levels, measure predicted-versus-true endpoint offsets, fit the scaling law, then test the fitted law on one real dataset with thin structures.
main_risk: Real anatomy confounds (branching, neighboring tissue) may swamp the clean phantom law.
default_community_belief: Errors at thin ends are attributed to class imbalance and resolution limits, assumed reducible only by higher resolution or more data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may use contextual continuation cues rather than local intensity, breaking any local threshold law.
fastest_falsification: Phantom-only version of the experiment runs in hours with an existing checkpoint.

one_line: Fine-tuned foundation models transfer an institution's contouring style to new anatomy more readily than they transfer anatomical accuracy.
problem: Institutions differ in systematic contouring style (tight versus generous margins); it is unknown whether adaptation learns anatomy or style.
core_hypothesis: Style is a low-dimensional, easily learnable bias, so a model fine-tuned on institution A applied at institution B will show a global signed volume bias matching A's style, even for organs absent from the fine-tuning set.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-institution evaluation will show a signed boundary offset that (a) has consistent sign across organs, (b) matches the sign of the source institution's style relative to the target, and (c) appears even on organs never seen during fine-tuning.
why_important: If style transfers globally, cross-site validation numbers conflate style mismatch with capability, and simple per-site bias correction could recover substantial performance.
why_possibly_novel: Site effects are usually modeled as image-domain shift; modeling them as annotation-style shift that generalizes across organs within a model is a distinct mechanism.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune on one institution's labels, evaluate signed surface distance per organ on another institution with different documented style, including held-out organ classes, and test for the consistent sign pattern.
main_risk: Requires two datasets with genuinely different, documented contouring conventions and overlapping organ sets.
default_community_belief: Cross-site performance drops are attributed to scanner and population shift in the images, not to transferable annotation style in the labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Style may be organ-specific rather than global, in which case unseen organs would show no bias.
fastest_falsification: Signed-distance audit of existing cross-site evaluation outputs, if paired-style datasets are already available.

one_line: Foundation-model confidence peaks on smooth intensity ramps, exactly where clinical boundary uncertainty is greatest, an inversion with measurable structure.
problem: Smooth transitions (edema, infiltration) are hard for clinicians but may be easy for edge-based models to commit to, creating a dangerous confidence inversion.
core_hypothesis: Model confidence is driven by local decision-margin in feature space, which is high on smooth monotonic ramps because any threshold yields a stable mask, so confidence and clinical uncertainty become inversely related on ramp-type boundaries specifically.
falsifiable_prediction: Partitioning boundary segments into step-type and ramp-type by intensity profile, ramp-type segments will show higher model confidence but higher inter-rater variance, yielding a negative confidence-to-ambiguity correlation restricted to ramps.
why_important: This would identify a specific, screenable boundary class where confidence-based review queues actively fail, with a concrete mitigation (profile-type detection).
why_possibly_novel: Boundary-type-conditional calibration analysis (step versus ramp) is a finer-grained question than global calibration studies.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Classify boundary voxels by fitted intensity-profile type on a multi-rater dataset and compare confidence and rater variance across types.
main_risk: Profile-type classification is itself noisy and may not cleanly separate the two regimes.
default_community_belief: Confidence errors are assumed uniform along boundaries, fixable by global temperature scaling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ramp regions may produce genuinely diffuse logits in modern architectures with strong augmentation, keeping confidence low there.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only stratified calibration analysis on one existing multi-rater dataset.

one_line: Models trained under two contouring conventions cannot interpolate to an intermediate instruction, revealing that convention is memorized, not parameterized.
problem: Ideally a model could be told how aggressive a margin to draw; whether current architectures represent convention as a controllable variable is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Convention is entangled in weights rather than represented as a latent control axis, so a model trained on two discrete conventions with condition codes will fail to produce sensible intermediate contours when given interpolated codes.
falsifiable_prediction: Given condition-code interpolation between tight and generous margin conventions, output contours will jump discontinuously between the two learned styles rather than move smoothly, as measured by mean signed distance versus code value.
why_important: Controllable margin aggressiveness would let one model serve multiple clinical protocols; demonstrating the failure motivates explicit convention-conditioning research.
why_possibly_novel: Treating annotation convention as an explicit conditioning axis and testing interpolation behavior is a designed probe rather than an observational study.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Relabel one organ under two margin rules, train with a scalar condition input, sweep the condition at test time, and plot signed distance versus condition value for smoothness.
main_risk: Failure to interpolate might be fixable trivially with more condition values, making the negative result weak.
default_community_belief: Conditioning inputs are assumed to give smooth control over output properties as they often do in generative models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distance-to-boundary is nearly linear in margin width, which is an easy function; the model may interpolate perfectly.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale training on a single organ with synthetic margin relabeling; one short training run.

one_line: Weighting training loss by rater-disagreement maps changes where models place boundaries but not aggregate Dice, exposing metric blindness to ambiguity handling.
problem: It is unclear whether incorporating known ambiguity into the loss changes model behavior in a way standard metrics can even detect.
core_hypothesis: Disagreement-weighted losses shift boundary placement toward consensus regions and soften commitments in ambiguity zones, but because ambiguous voxels are few, Dice and surface metrics remain statistically unchanged, hiding a real behavioral difference.
falsifiable_prediction: Two models trained with and without disagreement weighting will be indistinguishable in Dice yet significantly different in ambiguity-zone-restricted metrics and in agreement with held-out raters.
why_important: If true, the field's standard metrics cannot see the property that matters for ambiguity-aware deployment, and ambiguity-zone metrics need to become standard.
why_possibly_novel: The claim is about metric detectability of a training intervention, not about the intervention improving a headline number.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models on a multi-rater dataset with and without disagreement weighting, evaluate with global metrics and ambiguity-zone-restricted metrics, and test the dissociation.
main_risk: The intervention might change nothing at all, which is a publishable null but weaker.
default_community_belief: If a training change matters clinically, it should show up in Dice or surface distance; metric sufficiency is assumed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Surface-distance metrics may be sensitive enough near boundaries to capture the change after all.
fastest_falsification: One paired training run on an existing multi-rater dataset with a pre-registered ambiguity-zone metric.

one_line: Logit iso-contours of dense predictors carry recoverable sub-voxel boundary information that discrete masks discard.
problem: Clinical margins are specified in millimeters, often below voxel size; whether learned dense predictors encode sub-voxel boundary position in their continuous outputs is untested.
core_hypothesis: The pre-threshold logit field varies smoothly across the true boundary, so interpolated iso-contours estimate boundary position with sub-voxel accuracy relative to higher-resolution ground truth, beating the discrete mask by a measurable margin.
falsifiable_prediction: Using high-resolution acquisitions downsampled for inference, interpolated logit iso-contours will localize the boundary with lower error than the binarized mask boundary, and the gain will exceed what naive mask-based interpolation achieves.
why_important: Free sub-voxel accuracy from existing models would matter for volumetry of small structures and margin verification without any retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Sub-voxel evaluation of learned dense predictors against genuinely higher-resolution ground truth is rarely set up explicitly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Downsample high-resolution scans, run an existing model, compare iso-contour and mask-boundary localization error against the original-resolution labels.
main_risk: Downsampling simulation may not reflect true low-resolution acquisition physics, biasing the measured gain.
default_community_belief: Voxel resolution is treated as the hard floor of boundary accuracy; outputs are binarized before any geometric analysis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Logit slopes near boundaries may be governed by training-label voxelization noise rather than image evidence, containing no true sub-voxel signal.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only study on any high-resolution dataset with synthetic downsampling.

one_line: On core-versus-whole lesion tasks, foundation models select a fixed operating point on the local intensity distribution rather than understanding the task distinction.
problem: Tasks like enhancing-core versus whole-lesion segmentation require different semantic boundaries in the same image region; whether models represent the distinction or just different thresholds is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Models fine-tuned for nested targets implement approximately quantile thresholds on a shared saliency field, so their core and whole predictions are related by a monotone intensity remapping and fail together on lesions with atypical intensity ordering.
falsifiable_prediction: For lesions where the true core is not the brightest compartment (atypical enhancement), core predictions will systematically select the brightest compartment instead, and errors on core and whole tasks will be strongly correlated case-by-case.
why_important: Nested-target tasks are common in oncology; a shared-threshold mechanism predicts correlated failures that ensemble-style safety arguments would wrongly treat as independent.
why_possibly_novel: Testing whether nested-task heads share a single latent saliency axis via atypical-ordering cases is a mechanism-level probe, not a benchmark comparison.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify atypical-enhancement cases in a public lesion dataset, evaluate per-case correlation of core and whole errors, and test whether core masks track the brightest compartment.
main_risk: Atypical-ordering cases may be rare and hard to verify without expert review.
default_community_belief: Separate heads or prompts for nested subregions are assumed to learn distinct semantic definitions of each compartment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multi-channel MR input may give models genuinely different features per compartment, breaking the single-axis account.
fastest_falsification: Case-level error-correlation analysis on existing multi-compartment predictions.

one_line: Per-image intensity normalization in foundation-model pipelines discards absolute CT calibration, measurably hurting tasks that depend on Hounsfield semantics.
problem: CT is quantitatively calibrated (Hounsfield units carry tissue meaning), but standard foundation-model preprocessing normalizes each image independently, destroying the absolute scale.
core_hypothesis: Some segmentation distinctions (e.g., fluid versus soft tissue, fat-containing lesions) rely on absolute attenuation, so per-image normalization creates a specific error class that vanishes when absolute-HU information is restored as an input channel.
falsifiable_prediction: Errors concentrated on attenuation-defined distinctions will be significantly reduced by adding a fixed-window absolute-HU channel, while boundary-geometry errors remain unchanged; conversely, applying global HU shifts at test time will degrade normalized-input models much less than it should if they used absolute values.
why_important: This isolates a concrete, cheap-to-fix information loss in the dominant preprocessing convention, with implications for every CT foundation-model pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: The question targets which error class is caused by normalization, using intervention on input channels, rather than reporting an overall score difference.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or adapt paired models with and without an absolute-HU channel on one CT dataset, stratify errors into attenuation-defined versus geometry-defined classes, and compare the strata.
main_risk: Attenuation-defined error classes must be defined a priori and may be entangled with geometry.
default_community_belief: Intensity normalization is considered harmless standardization; performance differences are attributed to architecture and data scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may recover absolute scale from anatomical context (air, bone landmarks) making the explicit channel redundant.
fastest_falsification: Test-time HU-shift sensitivity analysis on an existing model: if predictions are invariant to physically meaningful shifts, absolute information is unused.

one_line: Window and level preprocessing choices dominate reported foundation-model medical performance more than model choice, but are rarely controlled.
problem: CT windowing decisions made before inference compress different tissue ranges; comparisons between models rarely hold windowing constant or optimize it per model.
core_hypothesis: The performance spread across reasonable windowing choices for a fixed model exceeds the spread across model families at fixed windowing, for low-contrast targets in particular.
falsifiable_prediction: A grid over clinically used window settings will produce a within-model performance range larger than the between-model range reported on the same tasks, and per-model optimal windows will differ, changing model rankings.
why_important: If windowing is the dominant factor, many published comparisons are confounded, and windowing should be treated as a learned or reported hyperparameter.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic windowing-sensitivity audits across foundation models are uncommon; the ranking-flip claim is directly testable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two or three public checkpoints over a windowing grid on one low-contrast CT task and compare within-model versus between-model variance.
main_risk: Effect may be small for models trained with heavy intensity augmentation.
default_community_belief: Preprocessing is standardized enough that reported differences reflect model capability.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern medical pipelines often use fixed conventions consistently, so real-world comparisons may already be fair.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only windowing grid on existing checkpoints; a few GPU-hours.

one_line: Foundation models cannot identify MR sequence type from image content alone, and their segmentation errors trace to sequence confusion.
problem: MR intensity meaning depends on the pulse sequence, which is metadata; models fed raw slices must infer the sequence implicitly, and failures of this inference are undocumented.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of foundation-model errors on multi-sequence MR corpora are sequence-confusion errors: the model applies the intensity semantics of the wrong sequence, and a linear probe on its features will show poor sequence identification exactly on the failing cases.
falsifiable_prediction: Cases where a sequence-identification probe on frozen features is wrong or uncertain will have significantly worse segmentation than probe-confident cases, matched for anatomy, and providing the true sequence label as input will preferentially fix those cases.
why_important: Sequence confusion is fixable with metadata conditioning; quantifying it separates a solvable failure source from genuine capability limits.
why_possibly_novel: Linking a feature-space probe failure to case-level segmentation failure with a metadata intervention is a causal chain rarely tested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a sequence probe on frozen features of a multi-sequence corpus, stratify segmentation error by probe confidence, then rerun with sequence conditioning to see targeted recovery.
main_risk: Sequence type correlates with site and protocol, confounding the stratification.
default_community_belief: Big models are assumed to infer sequence context effortlessly from global appearance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sequence identification may indeed be trivially easy, making probe accuracy near-perfect and the hypothesis moot.
fastest_falsification: The linear probe itself: if it achieves near-perfect accuracy on held-out sites, the confusion mechanism is implausible.

one_line: Ultrasound speckle is discriminative signal that foundation-model invariances destroy: speckle-preserving pipelines will beat speckle-suppressing ones on tissue-differentiation tasks.
problem: Speckle patterns in ultrasound carry tissue microstructure information, but pretraining and preprocessing (denoising, blurring, augmentation) treat them as noise.
core_hypothesis: For segmentation targets defined by tissue texture rather than borders, models whose training pipeline preserves speckle statistics will outperform those with speckle-destroying augmentation, and the gap will be absent for border-defined targets.
falsifiable_prediction: A two-by-two experiment (speckle-preserving versus destroying pipeline, texture-defined versus border-defined target) will show a significant interaction: pipeline matters for texture-defined targets only.
why_important: This tells the community whether ultrasound needs modality-specific pretraining invariances, a fundamental design question for medical foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: The interaction design distinguishes signal-destruction from generic augmentation effects, rather than reporting a single pipeline comparison.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune paired models on one ultrasound dataset with each pipeline for one texture-defined and one border-defined structure, and test the interaction term.
main_risk: Clean texture-defined segmentation targets with public labels are uncommon in ultrasound.
default_community_belief: Stronger augmentation and denoising invariances are assumed to broadly help medical transfer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep features may recover microstructure cues from residual low-frequency correlates of speckle even after suppression.
fastest_falsification: Frozen-feature probe comparison on speckle-preserved versus suppressed patches for a tissue-classification proxy task.

one_line: Under metal and beam-hardening artifacts, foundation models hallucinate plausible anatomy instead of expressing uncertainty, and hallucination rate scales with pretraining scale.
problem: Artifacts destroy image evidence locally; the failure mode of large pretrained models under evidence-free regions (guess versus abstain) is safety-critical and unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Larger pretraining instills stronger anatomical priors, so under artifact-corrupted regions bigger models produce more confident, more anatomically plausible, but not more accurate completions than smaller models, an inverse-scaling safety property.
falsifiable_prediction: Injecting simulated metal artifacts into scans with known ground truth, plausibility scores of predictions in corrupted regions will increase with model scale while accuracy in those regions stays flat, and confidence will not drop relative to uncorrupted regions.
why_important: Confident hallucination under artifacts is a worst-case clinical failure; showing it worsens with scale would challenge the assumption that bigger is safer.
why_possibly_novel: Inverse-scaling analysis for dense-prediction hallucination under physics-based corruption is a specific, mechanism-oriented safety question.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use an artifact simulator on clean labeled CT, evaluate small versus large checkpoints of one family on corrupted-region accuracy, confidence, and a plausibility measure (agreement with atlas).
main_risk: Simulated artifacts may differ from real ones in ways that change model behavior.
default_community_belief: Scale improves robustness monotonically, including under corruption.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Larger models may also have better uncertainty behavior, dropping confidence appropriately in corrupted regions.
fastest_falsification: Two-checkpoint comparison with a public artifact-simulation tool on one dataset.

one_line: Foundation-model feature quality degrades non-linearly with slice thickness, with a breakpoint set by pretraining resolution statistics rather than anatomy.
problem: Clinical archives contain a wide range of slice thicknesses; how transfer performance depends on resolution, and whether the dependence is model-intrinsic or anatomy-intrinsic, is not characterized.
core_hypothesis: Performance versus slice thickness follows a piecewise pattern with a model-specific breakpoint: above the breakpoint, features fall off a learned manifold and errors rise sharply; the breakpoint location is shared across anatomies for a given model but differs across models with different pretraining data.
falsifiable_prediction: Reconstructing the same raw acquisitions at multiple thicknesses, error-versus-thickness curves will show a common breakpoint across organs within one model, and the breakpoint will shift between models pretrained on different resolution distributions.
why_important: A model-intrinsic breakpoint tells deployers exactly which archive data a model can be trusted on, and motivates resolution-diverse pretraining.
why_possibly_novel: Separating model-intrinsic from anatomy-intrinsic resolution dependence via multi-reconstruction of identical acquisitions is a controlled design rarely executed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use one dataset with thin-slice acquisitions, simulate thicker reconstructions, evaluate two different checkpoints across organs, and test breakpoint consistency.
main_risk: Simulated thick slices approximate but do not equal native reconstructions.
default_community_belief: Resolution effects are assumed smooth and anatomy-driven: small things fail first, models differ little.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interpolation layers may make models genuinely resolution-agnostic, yielding smooth anatomy-driven curves only.
fastest_falsification: Error-versus-thickness curve for one organ and two models using synthetic downsampling.

one_line: Dose reduction degrades foundation-model segmentation before it degrades human-perceptible image quality, inverting the assumed safety margin.
problem: Low-dose CT protocols are chosen so images remain diagnostic to humans; whether learned dense predictors tolerate the same noise levels is an independent, untested question.
core_hypothesis: Foundation models rely on texture statistics that noise corrupts earlier than the structural cues humans use, so segmentation quality declines at noise levels still rated diagnostic, particularly for texture-dependent targets.
falsifiable_prediction: Across simulated dose levels, segmentation metrics will fall significantly at dose levels above the threshold where trained observers report diagnostic acceptability, with texture-dependent structures failing first.
why_important: Dose protocols optimized for human readers may silently break AI pipelines; quantifying the divergence sets evidence-based dose floors for AI-assisted workflows.
why_possibly_novel: Explicitly comparing the model degradation threshold against a human acceptability threshold on the same images frames it as a two-observer psychophysics problem.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply a validated low-dose simulation to labeled CT, measure model metrics across dose levels, and compare the model breakdown point with published or locally collected acceptability ratings on the same data.
main_risk: Human acceptability thresholds vary; a proxy (reader ratings from prior literature on the same simulation) may be contested.
default_community_belief: If an image is diagnostic for a radiologist, it is assumed adequate for AI inference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Heavy augmentation during training may make models more noise-tolerant than humans, reversing the ordering.
fastest_falsification: Dose-sweep inference with an existing simulator and checkpoint on one dataset.

one_line: MR undersampling artifacts create structured segmentation failures that image-domain fine-tuning cannot remove, because aliasing is non-local.
problem: Accelerated MR reconstruction leaves aliasing and blurring artifacts whose non-local structure differs fundamentally from the local noise models implicit in standard augmentation.
core_hypothesis: Because aliasing folds distant anatomy into the target region, image-domain models cannot learn to invert it from finite data; segmentation errors under acceleration will remain concentrated at alias-overlap locations after fine-tuning on accelerated images, whereas errors from local blur will be fixed.
falsifiable_prediction: After fine-tuning on retrospectively undersampled images, residual errors will co-localize with computable alias-fold positions significantly above chance, and this co-localization will not decrease with more fine-tuning data, unlike blur-induced errors.
why_important: This bounds what post-hoc adaptation can fix and argues that segmentation robustness to acceleration must be solved jointly with reconstruction.
why_possibly_novel: Predicting the spatial layout of irreducible errors from k-space sampling geometry is a physics-grounded, sharply testable claim.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrospectively undersample a labeled MR dataset with known trajectories, fine-tune at increasing data scale, and measure error co-localization with predicted alias positions versus data scale.
main_risk: Retrospective undersampling of magnitude images approximates true raw-data acceleration imperfectly.
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning on artifact-matched data is assumed sufficient to restore robustness to any reconstruction artifact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may learn alias-unfolding heuristics from context, since anatomy is highly structured and folds are partly predictable.
fastest_falsification: Error-localization analysis on one undersampling factor with a fixed fine-tuned model.

one_line: Eight-bit conversion in common foundation-model pipelines erases low-contrast lesions from the input, setting a hard recall ceiling invisible in aggregate metrics.
problem: Many pretrained-model pipelines convert 12-to-16-bit medical data to 8-bit RGB; for low-contrast targets the quantization may remove the discriminative signal entirely.
core_hypothesis: There exists a target-contrast threshold, computable from the quantization step, below which lesions become mathematically indistinguishable from background in the 8-bit input, so recall for such lesions is bounded by chance regardless of model quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Lesions whose native contrast falls below the computed quantization threshold will show near-zero recall in 8-bit pipelines and substantially higher recall in 16-bit-preserving pipelines, while high-contrast lesion recall will match between pipelines.
why_important: A provable input-information ceiling reframes some reported model failures as preprocessing bugs and gives an audit rule for any pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Deriving and empirically validating a per-lesion computable recall bound from bit-depth arithmetic is more precise than generic preprocessing warnings.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify lesions in one dataset by native contrast relative to the quantization step, evaluate identical models under 8-bit and 16-bit inputs, and compare recall in the below-threshold stratum.
main_risk: Windowing before quantization changes the effective threshold, so the audit must model the full pipeline.
default_community_belief: Bit-depth conversion is treated as an innocuous engineering detail with negligible effect after windowing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With appropriate windowing the quantization step may be finer than any clinically relevant contrast, making the below-threshold stratum empty.
fastest_falsification: Compute the contrast stratification and run paired inference; no training needed.

one_line: Physics-based augmentation changes which structures fail rather than uniformly improving robustness, so augmentation choice is a hidden clinical prioritization.
problem: Augmentation policies are chosen to maximize average robustness, but their per-structure effects in medical dense prediction are not decomposed.
core_hypothesis: Generic photometric augmentation and physics-based augmentation (noise, PSF, motion models) reallocate errors across structure types in systematically different ways, with near-zero average difference but large per-structure differences, meaning the augmentation choice implicitly decides which anatomy is protected.
falsifiable_prediction: Paired trainings differing only in augmentation family will show statistically indistinguishable mean Dice but significant, reproducible per-structure gains and losses with opposite signs for texture-dependent versus geometry-dependent structures.
why_important: If augmentation is a zero-sum reallocation at fixed capacity, robustness claims must be reported per structure, and safety-critical structures need explicitly matched augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: The zero-sum reallocation framing with a pre-registered structure typology is a sharper claim than augmentation A beats B.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models on one multi-organ dataset with each augmentation family, three seeds each, and test the interaction between augmentation family and structure type.
main_risk: Multiple seeds and trainings make this moderately expensive; effects may be seed-noise dominated.
default_community_belief: Better augmentation is assumed to be Pareto-improving across structures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With large capacity models, augmentation families may compose without trade-offs, giving genuine Pareto gains.
fastest_falsification: Reanalysis of any existing augmentation ablation at per-structure granularity, if such runs are available.

one_line: Foundation models conflate contrast-agent phases, and phase-swapped test cases reveal that vessel and lesion segmentation rely on phase-specific shortcuts.
problem: Contrast-enhanced CT and MR appearance depends strongly on injection phase; models trained on mixed-phase corpora may learn phase-conditional shortcuts that fail silently on unusual phases.
core_hypothesis: Models implicitly infer phase from global appearance and switch segmentation strategies accordingly; when phase cues are ambiguous or atypical, they apply the wrong strategy, producing characteristic errors (e.g., treating unenhanced vessels as absent).
falsifiable_prediction: On cases with atypical or mislabeled phase, error patterns will match the wrong-phase strategy (predictable direction, e.g., systematic under-segmentation of vessels in early phases), and conditioning the model on the true phase label will preferentially fix those cases.
why_important: Phase heterogeneity is ubiquitous in real archives; a strategy-switching account predicts when models fail and offers metadata conditioning as a cheap fix.
why_possibly_novel: Testing an internal strategy-switch mechanism via phase conditioning and directional error predictions goes beyond reporting cross-phase performance drops.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify a contrast-enhanced dataset by phase, evaluate directional error patterns on off-phase cases, and rerun with explicit phase conditioning to measure targeted recovery.
main_risk: Reliable phase labels are often missing or noisy in public data.
default_community_belief: Mixed-phase training is assumed to yield phase-invariant robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may genuinely learn phase-invariant anatomical features, with off-phase drops explained by lower contrast alone.
fastest_falsification: Directional-error audit on off-phase cases of an existing model.

one_line: Reconstruction-kernel texture is a stronger determinant of foundation-model segmentation quality than the anatomy being segmented, revealed by kernel-swapped paired reconstructions.
problem: The same CT raw data reconstructed with different kernels yields different texture; models may key on kernel texture as a shortcut, but the effect size relative to anatomical difficulty is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Variance in model performance attributable to reconstruction kernel exceeds variance attributable to patient anatomy for soft-tissue structures, because kernel texture shifts features off the training manifold globally.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired reconstructions of identical raw data, within-patient between-kernel performance differences will exceed between-patient within-kernel differences for soft-tissue structures, and a kernel classifier on model features will be near-perfect.
why_important: If kernel dominates anatomy, single-kernel benchmarks systematically overstate generalization, and kernel harmonization becomes a first-order deployment requirement.
why_possibly_novel: Using paired same-patient reconstructions to put kernel and anatomy variance on the same scale is a clean variance-decomposition design.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Obtain or reconstruct a paired-kernel dataset, run a fixed model on both arms, and compare the two variance components with a mixed-effects analysis.
main_risk: Paired-kernel public data is limited; simulation via kernel-transfer methods adds its own artifacts.
default_community_belief: Kernel differences are considered a minor nuisance handled by augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models trained on heterogeneous archives may already be kernel-invariant, making anatomy the dominant factor.
fastest_falsification: Within-versus-between variance comparison on any available paired-kernel set with an existing checkpoint.

one_line: Through-plane topological defects of slice-wise foundation models scale predictably with inter-slice anatomy decorrelation, giving a computable reliability map.
problem: 2D foundation models applied slice-by-slice to volumes produce 3D inconsistencies, but when and where these occur has not been reduced to a predictive law.
core_hypothesis: The rate of through-plane defects (disconnections, holes) at a given location is a function of the local through-plane image autocorrelation length relative to slice spacing, independent of organ identity, so a defect-probability map is computable from the image alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Defect locations across organs and datasets will be predicted by the autocorrelation-to-spacing ratio with high rank correlation, and organs will not add explanatory power once the ratio is controlled.
why_important: A label-free defect predictor tells users where 2D-model outputs need 3D repair, and quantifies exactly what 3D-native models buy.
why_possibly_novel: Reducing the 2D-versus-3D debate to a single measurable image statistic with out-of-organ generalization is a stronger claim than benchmark comparisons.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a slice-wise model on one volumetric dataset, detect topological defects, regress defect occurrence on the local autocorrelation ratio, and test organ-identity residual effects.
main_risk: Defect detection itself requires choices (connectivity rules) that could bias the regression.
default_community_belief: 3D consistency failures are seen as an unstructured downside of 2D models, fixable by post-processing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Defects may be driven by slice-level segmentation errors with no clean relation to through-plane statistics.
fastest_falsification: Single-dataset regression analysis with an existing 2D checkpoint.

one_line: Multi-slice context helps only until the anatomical correlation length is covered, after which added slices contribute nothing, a measurable saturation law.
problem: The community oscillates between 2D, 2.5D, and 3D architectures without a quantitative account of how much through-plane context dense prediction actually needs.
core_hypothesis: For each structure there is a context-saturation depth tied to its through-plane correlation length; performance versus number of input slices rises then plateaus at that depth, and the plateau point transfers across models.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping input-slab thickness for fixed architecture, per-structure performance curves will plateau at depths that correlate strongly with independently measured through-plane correlation lengths, and no structure will show meaningful gains beyond twice its correlation length.
why_important: This converts architecture choice from fashion into a per-task calculation, potentially saving large compute by right-sizing context.
why_possibly_novel: Positing and testing a transferable saturation law grounded in an anatomical statistic goes beyond ablation tables.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or adapt one model at several slab depths on a multi-organ dataset and fit plateau points against measured correlation lengths.
main_risk: Long-range global context (e.g., organ presence cues) could break the local-correlation account for some structures.
default_community_belief: More 3D context is assumed generally better, limited only by memory.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transformers may exploit distant slices in ways local correlation statistics do not capture, producing gains past the predicted plateau.
fastest_falsification: Slab-depth sweep on two structures with very different correlation lengths.

one_line: Video foundation models propagating masks through volumes fail exactly where anatomy changes faster than natural-video motion statistics, a quantifiable mismatch.
problem: Treating the z-axis as time lets video models propagate masks through slices, but anatomical slice-to-slice change is not motion and violates the temporal smoothness priors learned from video.
core_hypothesis: Propagation failures concentrate at locations where the slice-to-slice deformation field magnitude exceeds the displacement distribution typical of adjacent video frames, so a mismatch score computed from the volume predicts failure locations before running the model.
falsifiable_prediction: The pre-computed mismatch score will predict propagation-error locations with high precision, and failures will be reduced by resampling the volume to lower per-step change (finer spacing) even at fixed total information.
why_important: This turns an ad-hoc trick (video models on volumes) into a characterized tool with known validity conditions and a cheap pre-flight check.
why_possibly_novel: Deriving a failure predictor from the statistical mismatch between anatomical and video temporal dynamics is a mechanism-level analysis of a popular hack.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a video-based propagator on one volumetric dataset, compute per-location slice-change magnitude, and evaluate its precision-recall for predicting propagation breaks.
main_risk: The video model's internal robustness may exceed its pretraining statistics, weakening the mismatch account.
default_community_belief: Video propagation is assumed to work wherever slices look similar, without a quantitative validity criterion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failures may instead be driven by appearance novelty rather than change magnitude.
fastest_falsification: Correlation of break points with slice-change magnitude on existing propagation outputs.

one_line: Disagreement among axial, coronal, and sagittal inferences of the same 2D model is an accurate label-free voxel error estimator with a determinable exchange rate.
problem: Estimating where a slice-wise model errs without labels is unsolved in deployment; orthogonal-plane self-disagreement is cheap but its quantitative validity is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Because the three plane-wise inferences make partially independent errors, their disagreement approximates an internal ensemble variance whose relationship to true error is stable across datasets, enabling a calibrated error predictor from a one-time calibration.
falsifiable_prediction: The disagreement-to-error mapping fitted on one dataset will transfer to a different dataset and scanner with small calibration loss, outperforming single-plane confidence as an error predictor in both settings.
why_important: A transferable label-free error estimator enables automatic quality control gates for clinical pipelines at zero annotation cost.
why_possibly_novel: The claim of cross-dataset stability of the disagreement-error exchange rate is stronger and more useful than within-dataset correlation reports.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit disagreement-versus-error curves on dataset A, apply frozen to dataset B, and measure calibration transfer against a single-plane entropy baseline.
main_risk: Anisotropic acquisitions degrade coronal and sagittal inference unequally, entangling disagreement with resolution rather than error.
default_community_belief: Multi-view disagreement is used as a heuristic ensemble trick, not treated as a calibrated instrument.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Plane-wise errors may be strongly correlated (shared features), making disagreement blind to the dominant error component.
fastest_falsification: Two-dataset transfer test of the fitted exchange rate with an existing checkpoint.

one_line: Foundation models cannot complete anatomy beyond the imaged field of view, whereas small 3D-native models can, exposing absent volumetric shape priors.
problem: Truncated fields of view are common (large patients, protocol limits); whether models extrapolate organ shape beyond the image edge tests whether they possess true 3D shape priors or only appearance mapping.
core_hypothesis: 2D foundation models have no mechanism to represent out-of-field shape, so their organ-volume estimates on truncated scans are biased exactly by the truncated fraction; 3D models trained with shape-completion objectives will show partial correction, quantifying prior strength.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetically truncated volumes with known full ground truth, foundation-model volume error will equal the truncated fraction almost exactly (no completion), while shape-aware 3D baselines will recover a significant portion, and the gap will persist after fine-tuning the 2D model on truncated data.
why_important: Volume estimates drive clinical decisions; knowing that certain models never extrapolate defines when truncation invalidates their outputs.
why_possibly_novel: Using truncation response as an operational measure of internal shape-prior strength provides a scalar prior-strength metric comparable across models.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetically crop labeled volumes at multiple truncation levels, measure volume-recovery fraction per model, and compare model families.
main_risk: Whether models should extrapolate is task-dependent; clinical users may prefer non-extrapolation, complicating interpretation.
default_community_belief: Segmentation models are neither expected nor tested for out-of-field behavior; the property is unmeasured rather than known.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even 3D shape-aware models may fail to extrapolate under distribution shift, making the contrast empty.
fastest_falsification: Truncation sweep with two existing checkpoints on one organ.

one_line: Isotropic resampling before inference hurts foundation models on native anisotropic data, contrary to standard practice, because it destroys in-plane detail the models rely on.
problem: Pipelines routinely resample anisotropic medical volumes to isotropic spacing before inference, trading in-plane resolution against through-plane smoothness without evidence about what pretrained features prefer.
core_hypothesis: Foundation-model features are dominated by in-plane texture learned at high resolution, so preserving native in-plane resolution beats isotropic resampling for slice-wise inference, with the reverse holding only for genuinely 3D architectures.
falsifiable_prediction: A two-by-two evaluation (2D versus 3D model, native versus isotropic resampling) will show a significant interaction: 2D models better on native spacing, 3D models better on isotropic, with effect size largest for thin in-plane structures.
why_important: Resampling is a universal pipeline step; an interaction effect would mean current one-size-fits-all preprocessing systematically handicaps some model classes.
why_possibly_novel: The model-class-conditional resampling claim is more specific than existing preprocessing folklore and directly actionable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one 2D and one 3D checkpoint under both resampling schemes on one anisotropic dataset and test the interaction.
main_risk: Results may depend heavily on interpolation method, requiring careful control.
default_community_belief: Isotropic resampling is treated as a safe default that helps or at worst does not hurt.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models may be resolution-robust enough that resampling choice is second-order.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only two-by-two on existing checkpoints.

one_line: Foundation models ignore contralateral symmetry: occluding one body side leaves predictions on the other side unchanged, unlike human readers.
problem: Bilateral symmetry is a powerful anatomical prior used by clinicians (compare to the healthy side); whether learned dense predictors exploit it is unknown and testable by intervention.
core_hypothesis: Current models process anatomy locally enough that information from the contralateral side does not influence predictions, so symmetry-based error correction and asymmetry-based pathology detection are absent capabilities rather than emergent ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Masking or corrupting the contralateral side will not change predictions on the intact side beyond noise, and inserting synthetic asymmetric lesions will not raise local segmentation sensitivity relative to symmetric controls.
why_important: If symmetry is unused, an explicit symmetry-aware mechanism is a promising, anatomically grounded direction; if used, it constitutes an emergent 3D prior worth characterizing.
why_possibly_novel: Causal occlusion tests for symmetry use in dense medical prediction are rarely performed; most claims about context use are correlational.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paired inference with and without contralateral occlusion on bilateral organs, measuring prediction change on the intact side; complement with asymmetric-lesion insertion tests.
main_risk: Occlusion artifacts themselves may perturb global feature statistics, creating spurious sensitivity.
default_community_belief: Large receptive fields are assumed to implicitly exploit all available context including symmetry.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention layers may already move contralateral information, producing measurable occlusion sensitivity.
fastest_falsification: Contralateral-occlusion sensitivity measurement on one bilateral structure with an existing model.

one_line: Slice-shuffle invariance quantifies how much volumetric order information current pipelines actually use, and the answer is close to none for 2D-plus-stitching systems.
problem: Anatomy imposes strict slice ordering, but pipelines built from independent slice inference plus post-hoc stitching may use none of it; the field lacks a number for how much order information is exploited.
core_hypothesis: For 2D-plus-stitching pipelines, randomly permuting slices before inference and un-permuting outputs changes results only through stitching, giving a small, measurable order-information usage; genuinely 3D pipelines will show large degradation, making shuffle sensitivity a clean capability metric.
falsifiable_prediction: Shuffle sensitivity (performance drop under slice permutation) will be near zero for slice-wise pipelines, substantial for 3D pipelines, and will correlate across models with their advantage on through-plane-curved structures.
why_important: A single order-sensitivity number lets practitioners audit whether an expensive 3D architecture actually uses 3D structure or just burns memory.
why_possibly_novel: Proposing shuffle sensitivity as a standard capability audit for volumetric usage is a methodological contribution with immediate applicability.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure shuffle sensitivity for one 2D and one 3D pipeline on one dataset and correlate with per-structure advantages.
main_risk: The metric conflates order usage with adjacency usage; partial shuffles are needed to separate them.
default_community_belief: 3D architectures are assumed to use volumetric structure in proportion to their compute cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: 3D models may degrade under shuffle for trivial reasons (broken convolution statistics) rather than lost anatomy usage, inflating the metric.
fastest_falsification: Shuffle-sensitivity measurement is inference-only and runs in hours.

one_line: Tubular-tree breaks in stitched 2D foundation-model outputs follow a characteristic break-length distribution predictable from slice spacing and vessel angle.
problem: Vessel and airway trees segmented slice-wise then stitched exhibit breaks; treating break statistics as a predictable geometric phenomenon rather than random failure has not been done.
core_hypothesis: A break occurs when a branch's angle to the slice plane makes its cross-section drop below the model's in-plane detection threshold, so break probability per unit length is a computable function of local branch angle, radius, and slice spacing.
falsifiable_prediction: The fitted geometric model of break probability will predict held-out break locations across patients with high discrimination, and interventions that only change slice spacing will shift break statistics exactly as predicted.
why_important: Vascular connectivity drives downstream planning; a predictive break model enables targeted repair and principled acquisition-protocol choices.
why_possibly_novel: Reducing connectivity failures to an explicit geometric detection model with out-of-sample prediction is a physics-of-failure approach uncommon in segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one vascular dataset, extract centerlines, fit break probability versus angle, radius, and spacing, and validate on held-out patients and a second spacing.
main_risk: Stitching heuristics vary and may dominate breaks in ways the geometric model ignores.
default_community_belief: Vessel breaks are attributed to model weakness in general, to be fixed by better models or topological losses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Breaks may cluster at bifurcations for appearance reasons unrelated to slice geometry.
fastest_falsification: Angle-stratified break-rate analysis on existing vessel predictions.

one_line: Errors on thin structures are direction-dependent, aligned with the acquisition axis, and are not removed by isotropic resampling, revealing that the anisotropic PSF is baked into learned features.
problem: Resampling makes voxels isotropic but cannot restore lost through-plane frequency content; whether models behave as if data were isotropic after resampling is untested.
core_hypothesis: Model errors on thin structures will remain systematically larger along the original acquisition axis even after isotropic resampling, because the anisotropic PSF leaves directional signatures that features inherit; error anisotropy is thus an intrinsic marker of acquisition, not fixable by resampling.
falsifiable_prediction: Directional error decomposition will show excess error along the original through-plane axis post-resampling, and rotating volumes before inference will rotate the error anisotropy with the data, confirming it is data-borne rather than model-borne.
why_important: Deployment often hides acquisition anisotropy behind resampling; showing errors stay anisotropic warns against isotropy assumptions in downstream error models.
why_possibly_novel: The rotation-based attribution of error anisotropy to data versus model is a clean causal design.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate directional surface errors on resampled anisotropic data, then repeat with rotated inputs, and compare anisotropy axes.
main_risk: Interpolation artifacts from rotation may add their own directional errors.
default_community_belief: After isotropic resampling, error is implicitly treated as directionally unbiased.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For thick structures the PSF signature may be negligible, confining the effect to a small structure subset.
fastest_falsification: Directional error decomposition on one anisotropic dataset with existing predictions.

one_line: Token pruning and merging strategies in efficient 3D transformers preferentially discard exactly the tokens containing rare small lesions, making efficiency gains and small-lesion recall fundamentally coupled.
problem: 3D transformer efficiency methods drop or merge low-information tokens, but in medical volumes the most clinically important content (small lesions) is also the least globally salient.
core_hypothesis: Saliency-driven token reduction is anti-correlated with lesion presence for sub-threshold lesions, so recall of small lesions degrades super-linearly with token-reduction rate while organ Dice is flat, an efficiency-safety trade-off invisible in standard reporting.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping token-reduction rates, small-lesion recall will fall significantly at rates where mean Dice changes negligibly, and pruned-token maps will overlap lesion locations above chance.
why_important: Efficiency methods are being adopted for 3D medical transformers on cost grounds; quantifying the hidden recall cost is a deployment-safety necessity.
why_possibly_novel: Auditing token-selection mechanisms against clinical-importance maps rather than aggregate accuracy is a new evaluation axis for efficient architectures.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument one token-pruning 3D model, sweep reduction rate on a lesion dataset, and report per-size recall plus pruned-token-lesion overlap.
main_risk: Findings may be specific to one pruning criterion; several criteria must be covered for generality.
default_community_belief: Token reduction is presumed safe because aggregate metrics are stable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Lesions often have high local contrast, which may make their tokens salient enough to survive pruning.
fastest_falsification: Pruned-token-lesion overlap statistic on one model and dataset without any retraining.

one_line: At matched compute, 3D-native pretraining on modest medical data beats 2D foundation-model transfer only for structures with high through-plane curvature, a testable dichotomy that rationalizes the conflicting literature.
problem: Comparisons between 3D-from-scratch and 2D-transfer approaches disagree across papers; a structure-level moderator variable may explain the inconsistency.
core_hypothesis: The advantage of 3D-native representations is confined to structures whose through-plane geometry cannot be inferred slice-wise (high through-plane curvature or branching), while 2D transfer wins elsewhere because of larger pretraining; the sign of the difference is predictable per structure from a curvature statistic.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a multi-organ benchmark, the per-structure sign of the 3D-versus-2D performance difference will be predicted by through-plane curvature with high accuracy, and neither approach will dominate overall.
why_important: A validated moderator turns an unresolved architecture debate into a per-task decision rule and explains why existing studies conflict.
why_possibly_novel: The claim is not that either approach wins but that a measurable anatomical statistic determines the winner, which is a stronger, falsifiable structure-level theory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute-matched training of one 3D-native and one 2D-transfer pipeline on a multi-organ dataset, per-structure comparison against curvature statistics.
main_risk: Compute matching across paradigms is contentious and results may hinge on matching methodology.
default_community_belief: One paradigm is assumed generally superior, with disagreements attributed to implementation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Data scale rather than geometry may moderate the difference, in which case curvature would fail as a predictor.
fastest_falsification: Retrospective per-structure meta-analysis of existing public results against curvature statistics before any new training.

one_line: Prompt-placement sensitivity of promptable models grows with structure elongation following a measurable law, making tubular anatomy intrinsically prompt-hostile.
problem: Point and box prompts were designed for compact natural objects; medical anatomy includes extreme elongated and branching shapes where prompt semantics may break down.
core_hypothesis: The variance of output masks under prompt jitter scales with a shape-elongation statistic (e.g., skeleton length over mean radius), so interactive segmentation cost and reliability for a structure are predictable from its shape class before any user study.
falsifiable_prediction: Across structures spanning compact to tubular, prompt-jitter mask variance will increase monotonically with the elongation statistic, and the number of clicks needed to reach a target accuracy will follow the same ordering.
why_important: Predicting interaction cost from shape allows principled triage of which anatomy benefits from promptable tools versus fully automatic pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: A quantitative shape-to-prompt-sensitivity law is more general than per-dataset click-count reports.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Jittered-prompt inference across a shape-diverse structure set with one promptable model, regression of mask variance on elongation.
main_risk: Elongation may proxy for size or contrast, requiring careful covariate control.
default_community_belief: Prompt sensitivity is treated as a model deficiency to be engineered away, not a predictable function of target shape.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model-specific prompt encoders may dominate, making sensitivity idiosyncratic rather than shape-lawful.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only jitter study over ten structures of varying elongation.

one_line: Box prompts impose a compact-object prior: segmentation quality degrades predictably as the target's box-occupancy ratio falls, failing worst on thin diagonal structures.
problem: A bounding box around a thin diagonal structure is mostly background, so the box prompt's implicit assumption that the box is mostly object is violated in much of anatomy.
core_hypothesis: Promptable models decode box prompts under a learned occupancy prior from natural images, so mask quality is a monotone function of true occupancy ratio, and below a threshold the model segments a wrong compact object inside the box instead of the target.
falsifiable_prediction: Across structures, box-prompted accuracy will track occupancy ratio with a threshold below which failure becomes qualitative (wrong object class inside box), and re-parameterizing the prompt as a rotated or polyline region will remove most of the deficit.
why_important: Identifies a geometric interface flaw, not a capability flaw, implying prompt-geometry redesign rather than more medical fine-tuning is the fix.
why_possibly_novel: Attributing failures to prompt parameterization via occupancy analysis and testing geometric prompt alternatives isolates the interface as the causal factor.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify box-prompted performance by occupancy ratio on one dataset, then compare against rotated-box or scribble prompts at matched interaction budget.
main_risk: Occupancy correlates with thinness and contrast, needing multivariate analysis.
default_community_belief: Box prompts are considered a robust universal interface transferring cleanly to medical images.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may attend to interior evidence and ignore box shape statistics, making occupancy irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: Occupancy-stratified evaluation on existing box-prompted predictions.

one_line: Negative clicks are interpreted geometrically (push boundary away) not semantically (exclude tissue class), so excluding pathology from an organ mask fails in a characteristic way.
problem: Clinicians often need masks like organ-excluding-tumor; whether negative prompts communicate semantic exclusion or merely local boundary displacement determines if promptable models can express such targets.
core_hypothesis: Negative clicks act as local geometric repellers in current models, so excluding a spatially distributed tissue class (multifocal tumor) requires clicks near every focus, and a single semantic exclusion cannot be communicated regardless of click count at one focus.
falsifiable_prediction: Click-count to achieve pathology exclusion will scale linearly with number of pathology foci, and clicks on one focus will produce no exclusion at untouched foci even when the foci are visually identical, demonstrating absent semantic generalization of negatives.
why_important: Semantic exclusion is a core clinical requirement; documenting its absence defines a concrete capability gap and an evaluation task for next-generation interactive models.
why_possibly_novel: Testing whether prompt information generalizes across the image (semantic) versus staying local (geometric) is a designed probe of prompt semantics rarely made explicit.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multifocal-lesion cases, apply negative clicks at a subset of foci and measure exclusion at untouched foci versus locality baseline.
main_risk: Interpretation depends on model internals possibly varying widely across promptable architectures.
default_community_belief: Interactive models are assumed to infer user intent from a few clicks, including class-level exclusions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention mechanisms may propagate negative-click features to similar regions, giving partial semantic behavior.
fastest_falsification: Untouched-focus exclusion measurement on a handful of multifocal cases with an existing model.

one_line: Iterative click refinement converges to the prompting user's personal contouring bias, not toward consensus truth, making interactive accuracy an interaction-style artifact.
problem: Interactive segmentation is evaluated as if refinement approaches ground truth, but each correction click injects the corrector's own style, and the limit of this process is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: The fixed point of iterative correction is the corrector's personal contour distribution: models refined with clicks from rater A converge to A-style masks that diverge from consensus by A's known bias, so interactive gains partly re-encode individual style rather than accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Simulating correction policies derived from different raters' contours, final masks will classify by simulated rater identity with high accuracy, and final distance-to-consensus will be bounded below by each rater's own distance-to-consensus.
why_important: Interactive tools are marketed as accuracy multipliers; if they are style amplifiers, multi-user clinical workflows inherit inter-user variability rather than removing it.
why_possibly_novel: Analyzing the fixed point of human-in-the-loop refinement as a function of corrector identity reframes interactive evaluation methodology.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Derive simulated correction policies from a multi-rater dataset, run iterative refinement per policy, and test identity classification and consensus-distance bounds on final masks.
main_risk: Simulated correction policies may not capture real click behavior; a small real-user validation may be needed eventually.
default_community_belief: More correction clicks monotonically approach ground truth; user identity is treated as noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model shape priors may dominate late refinement, pulling all users toward the same attractor.
fastest_falsification: Rater-conditioned refinement simulation on one multi-rater dataset.

one_line: Clicks-to-target-accuracy follows a power law in a structure-complexity statistic, giving each model a measurable interaction exponent that summarizes its medical usability.
problem: Interactive evaluations report clicks for specific datasets, but no transferable law relates structure complexity to interaction cost, so results do not generalize across anatomy.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed model, expected clicks to reach a fixed accuracy scales as a power law in a complexity statistic (e.g., boundary length over area or genus-adjusted skeleton complexity), with a model-specific exponent that ranks models consistently across datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting the law on one anatomy set will predict click counts on unseen anatomies within tight error, and model ranking by exponent will be stable across datasets even when absolute clicks differ.
why_important: A validated interaction law converts fragmented click benchmarks into a single transferable usability score, and exposes whether interactive progress is real or dataset-specific.
why_possibly_novel: Positing scaling structure in human-in-the-loop cost, analogous to scaling laws in training compute, applies a quantitative lens to interface evaluation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulated-click protocol over a structure-diverse corpus, per-model power-law fits, held-out anatomy prediction test.
main_risk: Simulated clickers may distort the law relative to human behavior.
default_community_belief: Interaction cost is assumed idiosyncratic per dataset, summarized only by mean click counts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Click cost may be dominated by a few catastrophic-failure cases, breaking any smooth law.
fastest_falsification: Power-law fit quality check on one model across ten structures.

one_line: Given one ambiguous point in nested anatomy, foundation models choose the granularity level whose size matches natural-image object statistics, not the clinically salient level.
problem: A single click inside a tumor inside an organ inside a cavity is compatible with several targets; the model's granularity choice reveals its ontological prior, which for medical use may be systematically wrong.
