core_hypothesis: Ambiguity resolution follows a learned object-size prior from pretraining: the chosen mask level clusters near the pixel-area distribution typical of pretraining objects, so on large-organ contexts models under-select the clinically default structure.
falsifiable_prediction: Across nested contexts, the selected granularity will be predicted by proximity of candidate mask areas to a fixed model-specific preferred area, and rescaling the same image will shift the choice accordingly, proving the prior is size-based rather than semantic.
why_important: Granularity errors are silent (masks look valid); understanding the selection mechanism enables both a warning system and better multi-mask interface design.
why_possibly_novel: The image-rescaling intervention cleanly separates size-prior from semantic-prior explanations of ambiguity resolution.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Single-point prompts on nested structures at multiple image scales, tracking which level is selected versus mask area.
main_risk: Multi-mask outputs partially mitigate this; the analysis must target the ranked-first mask and the ranking scores.
default_community_belief: Ambiguity handling via multi-mask outputs is considered adequate, and selection is assumed loosely semantic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuned medical variants may have overwritten the size prior with dataset-specific defaults.
fastest_falsification: Rescaling experiment on a handful of nested-anatomy cases with an existing promptable model.

one_line: For nameable pathologies, a single geometric click beats any text prompt in current medical vision-language segmentation, quantifying how weak language grounding is relative to trivial spatial evidence.
problem: Text-promptable segmentation promises hands-free clinical use, but its value relative to minimal geometric interaction has not been established as an exchange rate.
core_hypothesis: Current text grounding in medical dense prediction contributes less target information than one well-placed click, so the click-equivalent value of a full clinical description is below one click for most findings, exposing text conditioning as presently decorative.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched evaluations, text-only prompting will underperform single-click prompting on nearly all finding types, and adding text to a click will improve over click-only by a margin smaller than adding a second click.
why_important: The click-equivalence framework prices language grounding progress in intuitive units, revealing whether text conditioning is worth its engineering cost in clinical interfaces.
why_possibly_novel: Measuring language value in units of interaction clicks provides a common currency absent from current text-versus-visual prompting comparisons.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three-arm evaluation (text-only, click-only, click-plus-text) on one report-linked dataset with matched targets.
main_risk: Result depends on text-prompt quality; prompts must be systematically constructed from reports to avoid strawmanning.
default_community_belief: Text promptability is presented as a major capability axis approaching geometric prompting in utility.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For findings invisible without prior knowledge (subtle diffuse disease), text may exceed one click decisively.
fastest_falsification: Click-versus-text arm comparison on an existing text-promptable medical checkpoint.

one_line: Segment-everything modes miss pathology at rates predicted by a visual-saliency model, showing automatic mask proposal inherits a saliency prior misaligned with clinical importance.
problem: Prompt-free whole-image mask generation is used for annotation bootstrapping, but its recall structure over clinically important versus salient regions is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Mask-proposal recall for a finding is predictable from a generic saliency score of that finding, so low-saliency pathology (isointense lesions, flat infiltration) is systematically absent from proposals, and the miss set is stable across model seeds because it is prior-driven.
falsifiable_prediction: Proposal recall versus saliency score will show strong positive dependence, misses will be reproducible across runs and model variants far above chance, and clinical-importance scores will add no predictive power once saliency is controlled.
why_important: Annotation pipelines seeded by mask proposals will systematically never label what matters most clinically, quietly propagating the saliency prior into future training data.
why_possibly_novel: Framing proposal misses as a reproducible, predictable prior rather than stochastic failure, and testing the data-flywheel contamination consequence, connects interface behavior to dataset evolution.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run segment-everything on a lesion dataset, regress per-lesion recall on saliency versus clinical grading, and measure miss-set overlap across variants.
main_risk: Choice of saliency model injects its own assumptions; several saliency definitions should be tested.
default_community_belief: Missed proposals are treated as random capacity limits, recoverable by lowering thresholds.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Threshold sweeps may recover low-saliency findings at acceptable false-positive cost, making the miss structure soft rather than hard.
fastest_falsification: Saliency-stratified recall analysis of existing proposal outputs on one dataset.

one_line: Cross-slice prompt propagation error compounds multiplicatively with distance, defining a maximum trustworthy propagation range measurable per anatomy.
problem: Interactive volumetric workflows prompt on sparse slices and propagate; whether error accumulates additively, multiplicatively, or saturates determines safe slice-sampling protocols, and this is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Propagation behaves like a noisy dynamical system with per-step error amplification greater than one in unstable anatomical regions, so error versus propagation distance is exponential there and near-linear in stable regions, yielding a computable per-region safe range.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting error-versus-distance curves per region, unstable regions (high slice-to-slice change) will show exponential fits significantly better than linear, and predicted safe ranges will transfer to held-out patients.
why_important: Safe-range maps convert interactive volumetry from folklore slice spacing to a principled protocol with quantified risk.
why_possibly_novel: Modeling propagation as a measurable dynamical system with regional stability analysis imports a control-theory lens into interactive segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Prompt at one slice, propagate bidirectionally, measure error growth against distance across regions on one volumetric dataset.
main_risk: Error growth may be dominated by rare discrete failures rather than smooth dynamics, favoring survival-analysis over curve fitting.
default_community_belief: Propagation quality is assumed roughly uniform, with fixed slice-interval recommendations used everywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern memory-based propagators may recover from local errors, giving saturating rather than exponential curves.
fastest_falsification: Error-growth curve fitting on one anatomy with an existing propagation model.

one_line: The spatial distribution of effective prompts reveals what a foundation model considers an object in medical images, providing an interpretability tool for its medical ontology.
problem: We lack tools to inspect what object concept a promptable model imposes on medical images; effective-prompt geography (which click locations yield stable coherent masks) may expose it.
core_hypothesis: Clustering prompt locations by their induced mask outcomes yields a partition of the image into the model's implicit object regions, and this partition aligns with intensity-homogeneous regions rather than anatomical entities, quantifying the ontology gap.
falsifiable_prediction: The implicit partition will match intensity clustering significantly better than it matches anatomical label boundaries, and the mismatch magnitude will predict zero-shot segmentation failure per structure.
why_important: A measurable ontology gap explains and predicts zero-shot behavior, and provides a target metric for medical adaptation beyond task accuracy.
why_possibly_novel: Using dense prompt-response mapping as a model-ontology microscope is an interpretability method specific to promptable dense predictors.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dense grid prompting on sample volumes, spectral clustering of mask outcomes, quantitative comparison against intensity clusters and anatomy labels.
main_risk: Computationally heavy; grid resolution trade-offs may blur the partition.
default_community_belief: Zero-shot medical weakness is described at task level; the internal object ontology is not measured directly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The partition may be prompt-encoder-specific noise rather than a stable ontology, failing reproducibility checks.
fastest_falsification: Partition stability and intensity-alignment test on a few volumes.

one_line: Clinicians place prompts precisely where they are uncertain, which is where models are also least reliable, so real interactive performance is bounded by correlated human-model failure.
problem: Interactive evaluation assumes prompts carry reliable information, but clinical users prompt most in regions of their own uncertainty, potentially injecting noise exactly where models need signal.
core_hypothesis: Human prompt placement density correlates positively with local ambiguity, and model prompt-value (accuracy gain per prompt) correlates negatively with ambiguity, so the realized clinical gain from interaction is substantially below simulated-oracle estimates due to this correlation structure.
falsifiable_prediction: Using recorded or realistically modeled human click distributions, per-click accuracy gain will be significantly lower than with standard simulated clickers, with the deficit proportional to the ambiguity-correlation strength.
why_important: This quantifies a structural optimism bias in the entire interactive-segmentation evaluation literature and motivates ambiguity-aware prompt guidance.
why_possibly_novel: The correlated-failure account of human-AI interaction is a systems-level hypothesis absent from standard per-component evaluation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare per-click gains between center-click simulation and an ambiguity-weighted click model calibrated on multi-rater data; a small recorded-click study strengthens it later.
main_risk: Without real click recordings the click model is an assumption; the initial result is conditional on it.
default_community_belief: Simulated-click benchmarks are assumed to approximate clinical interactive utility well.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Clinicians may prompt strategically in confident regions to anchor the model, reversing the correlation.
fastest_falsification: Gain comparison between click simulators of different ambiguity weighting on one dataset.

one_line: Standard center-click simulation overestimates interactive performance because real boundary-focused clicking interacts destructively with prompt encoders, a measurable simulator-validity failure.
problem: Nearly all interactive-segmentation results rest on simulated clickers; the sensitivity of conclusions to the simulator's click-placement policy is rarely reported.
core_hypothesis: Model performance is highly sensitive to click placement policy, and policies matching plausible human behavior (boundary-adjacent, error-directed) yield materially lower and differently-ranked results than center-of-error policies, meaning simulator choice silently determines leaderboards.
falsifiable_prediction: Across several models, switching click policy from center-of-mass to boundary-adjacent will change absolute performance substantially and alter model rankings, with rank instability exceeding seed noise.
why_important: If leaderboards are simulator artifacts, method progress claims in interactive medical segmentation need re-examination under standardized multi-policy reporting.
why_possibly_novel: Treating the click simulator as an experimental instrument requiring validity analysis applies measurement science to a taken-for-granted component.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-policy click simulation across three promptable models on one dataset, rank-stability analysis versus seed baseline.
main_risk: Without ground-truth human behavior, which policy is more valid remains partially arguable.
default_community_belief: Click-simulation details are treated as inconsequential implementation choices.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robust prompt encoders may make all reasonable policies equivalent, confirming simulator adequacy.
fastest_falsification: Two-policy comparison on one model and dataset, one afternoon of inference.

one_line: Foundation-model features encode acquisition site so strongly that site is linearly decodable better than anatomy, and site-feature removal changes which cases fail, not just averages.
problem: Cross-site degradation is documented at the score level, but the representational basis (how dominantly site is encoded relative to task signal) and its causal role in specific failures are not established.
core_hypothesis: In frozen foundation-model features, site identity occupies a high-variance linear subspace; projecting it out changes predictions mainly on cases whose errors were site-driven, so the intervention reallocates errors in a diagnosable way rather than uniformly improving scores.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear site decoding from features will exceed linear anatomy decoding accuracy; site-subspace removal will flip outcomes on an identifiable case subset (site-atypical appearance) while leaving typical cases unchanged.
why_important: Distinguishing site-driven from capability-driven failures per case enables targeted harmonization and honest cross-site claims.
why_possibly_novel: The causal projection intervention with case-level failure reallocation analysis goes beyond correlational site-probe studies.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train linear probes for site and anatomy on frozen features from a multi-site corpus, apply site-subspace projection, and analyze per-case prediction changes.
main_risk: Linear subspace removal may damage entangled task features, confounding interpretation.
default_community_belief: Site effects are seen as image-level nuisances best fixed by input harmonization, not as dominant feature-space structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In strongly fine-tuned models, site information may already be suppressed below anatomy signal.
fastest_falsification: Probe-accuracy comparison on frozen features of one multi-site dataset.

one_line: Burned-in overlays (rulers, annotations, device text) act as spatial anchors for foundation models: moving them moves the masks.
problem: Clinical images carry overlays whose spatial correlation with anatomy (positioning conventions) may be exploited as shortcuts by pretrained models; the causal effect has not been isolated.
core_hypothesis: Models use overlay positions as landmarks for spatial priors, so synthetically translating or removing overlays will cause measurable mask displacement or degradation even though no anatomical pixel changed.
falsifiable_prediction: Overlay-translation interventions will shift predicted masks in the translation direction above noise floor for a nontrivial case fraction, and overlay removal will degrade cases from overlay-rich training domains more than others.
why_important: Overlay anchoring is an invisible deployment hazard: a PACS configuration change could silently degrade a cleared model.
why_possibly_novel: Causal intervention on overlays for dense prediction, measuring geometric mask displacement rather than score change, directly demonstrates the shortcut mechanism.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Programmatic overlay translation and removal on an ultrasound or radiograph dataset, paired inference, displacement analysis.
main_risk: Inpainting used for removal introduces its own artifacts; translation tests avoid this but cover less.
default_community_belief: Overlays are assumed ignored by models as irrelevant clutter, or at worst mild noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation objectives are spatially dense and local, possibly making global anchor cues less useful than in classification.
fastest_falsification: Overlay-translation paired inference on a few hundred cases.

one_line: Foundation models carry a field-of-view position prior: identical anatomy at unusual image positions is segmented worse, quantified by crop-shift invariance testing.
problem: Organ positions within standard fields of view are highly regular, so models can learn absolute-position priors that fail on nonstandard positioning (trauma, pediatric, surgical planning).
core_hypothesis: A significant component of segmentation accuracy is attributable to absolute position within the input frame; controlled crop-shifting that relocates anatomy without changing content will degrade accuracy proportionally to shift distance from canonical position.
falsifiable_prediction: Accuracy versus positional shift will decline monotonically, positional sensitivity will be larger for foundation models pretrained with center-biased data than for convolutional baselines, and padding-based re-centering at inference will recover most of the loss.
why_important: Position priors create hidden failure modes for exactly the nonstandard cases where clinical stakes are often highest, and the fix (re-centering) is trivial once diagnosed.
why_possibly_novel: Comparing positional-sensitivity profiles across architecture families as a pretraining-artifact signature is a targeted robustness decomposition.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Crop-shift sweep on one dataset with two model families, accuracy-versus-shift curves, re-centering recovery test.
main_risk: Crop-shifting changes visible context, requiring careful padding design to isolate position from context loss.
default_community_belief: Translation robustness is assumed from augmentation and architecture, making position effects negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Windowed attention and augmentation pipelines may have removed absolute-position dependence.
fastest_falsification: Accuracy-versus-shift curve on one organ, inference only.

one_line: Pediatric failure of adult-trained foundation models is mostly a scale prior, not an anatomy gap: metric rescaling recovers a large share, and the unrecovered residue localizes to genuinely developmental structures.
problem: Models trained on adults degrade on children, but the causes (size, proportions, developmental anatomy, protocol) are entangled, blocking principled fixes.
core_hypothesis: The dominant failure factor is absolute physical scale mismatch with the learned prior; resampling pediatric scans so structures match adult metric sizes will recover most performance, and remaining errors will concentrate on structures with true developmental differences, yielding a decomposition of the pediatric gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Scale-normalized inference will close a large, quantifiable fraction of the pediatric gap; residual error will be spatially concentrated in developmentally distinct regions rather than uniformly distributed.
why_important: A validated decomposition tells the community whether pediatric AI needs new data (anatomy gap) or just scale-aware inference (prior gap), with major data-collection cost implications.
why_possibly_novel: The rescaling intervention as a causal decomposition tool for the pediatric gap turns a demographic observation into a mechanism experiment.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paired inference on pediatric data with and without metric scale normalization against age-specific labels, residual-error localization analysis.
main_risk: Interpolation artifacts from aggressive rescaling could mask or mimic recovery.
default_community_belief: Pediatric failure is attributed broadly to distribution shift requiring dedicated pediatric training data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Proportional differences (not just scale) may dominate, limiting recovery from uniform rescaling.
fastest_falsification: Rescaled-inference comparison on one pediatric dataset with an adult-trained model.

one_line: Lesion-segmentation false-positive rates of foundation models scale with training-set lesion prevalence, making screening-population deployment quantifiably miscalibrated at the population level.
problem: Benchmarks are enriched for pathology, while screening populations are mostly healthy; how the learned prevalence prior distorts dense predictions under prevalence shift is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Dense predictors internalize the training prevalence as a prior on lesion presence per image region, so false-positive area on healthy scans is an increasing function of training prevalence, and prevalence-matched recalibration of the decision threshold recovers most of the excess.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained at different lesion prevalences (subsampled corpora) will show monotonically increasing healthy-scan false-positive area; a single global threshold shift fitted on a small healthy set will remove a predictable fraction of it.
why_important: Population-level false-positive load determines screening viability; a quantitative prevalence law enables pre-deployment correction instead of post-hoc surprise.
why_possibly_novel: Treating training prevalence as a controllable experimental variable for dense prediction, with a recalibration transfer test, is a designed causal study of an assumed-but-unmeasured effect.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models on prevalence-controlled subsets of one lesion dataset, evaluate on held-out healthy scans, fit and test threshold recalibration.
main_risk: Prevalence manipulation also changes data volume; matched-size controls are required.
default_community_belief: Prevalence effects are acknowledged for classification but dense segmentation is assumed to be evidence-driven per voxel and largely immune.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Voxel-level evidence may indeed dominate priors in dense models, making the prevalence effect negligible.
fastest_falsification: Healthy-scan false-positive comparison between two existing checkpoints trained on corpora of known different prevalence.

one_line: Resampling-software fingerprints (interpolation signatures) are detectable by foundation models and exploited as dataset shortcuts, inflating within-benchmark generalization claims.
problem: Different preprocessing stacks leave characteristic interpolation and anti-aliasing signatures; if models detect them, benchmark splits sharing a pipeline overestimate real-world transfer.
core_hypothesis: Models can classify the preprocessing stack from images at high accuracy, and part of measured cross-dataset degradation is pipeline mismatch rather than acquisition shift, demonstrable by re-processing target data through the source pipeline and observing recovery.
falsifiable_prediction: Pipeline classification from frozen features will be far above chance; re-processing a target dataset through the source pipeline will recover a significant fraction of the cross-dataset gap without touching acquisition differences.
why_important: Separating pipeline shift from true acquisition shift changes how transfer results are interpreted and offers a zero-training mitigation (pipeline standardization).
why_possibly_novel: The pipeline re-processing recovery experiment cleanly isolates a shift source that is usually lumped into scanner effects.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe pipeline classification on features; re-process one target dataset with the source pipeline and compare transfer gaps.
main_risk: Access to the exact source pipeline may be incomplete, weakening the recovery test.
default_community_belief: Cross-dataset gaps are attributed to scanners and populations; preprocessing is assumed harmonized enough.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interpolation signatures may be too weak post-augmentation to be either detectable or exploitable.
fastest_falsification: Pipeline-classifier probe on frozen features of two datasets.

one_line: Medical shortcut features form a stable exploitation hierarchy: models rely on them in a consistent order, and knocking out one shortcut shifts reliance to the next, not to anatomy.
problem: Shortcuts (overlays, field of view, kernel texture, noise signatures) are studied one at a time; whether models exploit them in a systematic preference order, and what happens upon removal, is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Shortcut reliance follows an availability-times-simplicity hierarchy that is consistent across model seeds; sequential knockout experiments will show reliance cascading down the hierarchy, with anatomy-based prediction emerging only after all cheap shortcuts are removed.
falsifiable_prediction: Across seeds, the measured reliance order will be identical; each knockout will increase reliance on the next shortcut (measured by sensitivity tests) rather than increasing anatomy reliance, until the final knockout.
why_important: A cascade model of shortcut learning explains why single-shortcut mitigations underdeliver and argues for joint shortcut removal in medical training protocols.
why_possibly_novel: The hierarchy-and-cascade framing with sequential causal knockouts is a systems-level theory of shortcut learning rather than a catalog of instances.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a controlled corpus with three insertable shortcuts, train with sequential knockouts, measure reliance by targeted sensitivity probes at each stage.
main_risk: Synthetic shortcut insertion may not reproduce natural shortcut statistics, limiting external validity.
default_community_belief: Shortcut learning is treated case-by-case; removing an identified shortcut is assumed to redirect capacity to the true signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reliance order may be seed-dependent and chaotic, refuting a stable hierarchy.
fastest_falsification: Two-shortcut knockout study on a small controlled corpus.

one_line: Natural-image corruption robustness does not rank-transfer to medical corruptions: checkpoints ordered by natural robustness reorder under physics-based medical perturbations.
problem: Practitioners select robust checkpoints using natural-image robustness scores, implicitly assuming rank transfer to medical corruption types, which has not been verified for dense prediction.
core_hypothesis: Medical corruptions (noise from dose, motion, susceptibility, metal) stress different invariances than natural corruption suites, so robustness rankings across checkpoints will show low rank correlation between the two corruption families, invalidating checkpoint selection by natural robustness.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a set of public checkpoints, Spearman correlation between natural-corruption robustness rank and medical-corruption robustness rank will be low, with specific inversions where natural-robust models are medically fragile.
why_important: Checkpoint selection is a high-leverage, low-cost decision; showing rank non-transfer redirects selection practice toward medical-specific robustness testing.
why_possibly_novel: Rank-transfer analysis between corruption families for dense medical prediction, rather than average-robustness reporting, targets the actual decision practitioners make.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a checkpoint set under a natural corruption suite and a physics-based medical corruption suite on one task, compare rankings.
main_risk: Result depends on the medical corruption suite composition; suite must be pre-registered and physics-grounded.
default_community_belief: Robustness is assumed to be a general model property that transfers across corruption domains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robustness may stem from generic feature smoothness that helps under any corruption, preserving ranks.
fastest_falsification: Two-suite evaluation of five checkpoints on one dataset, inference only.

one_line: After image harmonization, the residual cross-site gap concentrates in a small set of structure types, showing harmonization fixes appearance shift but not representation-fragility shift.
problem: Harmonization methods report average gap reduction, but whether the residual gap is uniform or structure-concentrated determines what problem remains to be solved.
core_hypothesis: Harmonization removes global appearance mismatch, so the residual gap is dominated by structures whose features are intrinsically fragile (thin, low-contrast, high-variability), producing a heavy-tailed residual-gap distribution over structures that is consistent across harmonization methods.
falsifiable_prediction: Post-harmonization per-structure gap distributions will be heavy-tailed with the same top structures across different harmonization methods, and the tail structures will be predictable from fragility statistics (size, contrast, shape variability).
why_important: If the residual is structure-concentrated and predictable, cross-site research should shift from global harmonization to structure-targeted robustness, a different research program.
why_possibly_novel: Characterizing the invariant residual across harmonization methods identifies what harmonization fundamentally cannot fix, a question above any single method paper.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply two harmonization methods on one multi-site dataset, compute per-structure residual gaps, test cross-method rank agreement and fragility-statistic prediction.
main_risk: Requires multi-site data with consistent multi-structure labels, which constrains dataset choice.
default_community_belief: Better harmonization is expected to asymptotically close the cross-site gap for all structures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Residual gaps may reflect site-specific label styles rather than model fragility, changing the interpretation entirely.
fastest_falsification: Per-structure residual-gap analysis on existing harmonization outputs.

one_line: Under site shift, dense-prediction confidence stays flat while error rises, and the miscalibration is worse than in classification because spatial correlations hide the drift.
problem: Calibration under distribution shift is studied for classification; dense prediction adds spatially correlated errors whose interaction with confidence estimation is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation confidence is dominated by local texture typicality, which harmonizes quickly across sites, while errors are driven by subtler feature drift, so confidence-error correlation degrades with shift magnitude faster in dense prediction than in matched classification tasks on the same images.
falsifiable_prediction: Across sites ordered by shift magnitude, dense calibration error will grow faster than classification calibration error computed from the same backbone on the same cases, and voxelwise confidence maps will fail to flag the site-shift-induced error regions.
why_important: Confidence-gated deployment is a common safety plan; showing it fails specifically and more severely for dense prediction under site shift undermines a widespread assumption with a concrete measurement.
why_possibly_novel: The dense-versus-classification calibration comparison on matched data isolates what spatial structure does to shift miscalibration.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-site evaluation of one backbone with both a dense head and a classification head, calibration-versus-shift curves for both.
main_risk: Defining a fair matched classification task on the same data requires care.
default_community_belief: Calibration findings from classification are assumed to carry over qualitatively to segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense predictions aggregate many voxels, which may average out miscalibration and make segmentation better calibrated under shift, not worse.
fastest_falsification: Calibration-versus-shift comparison on one multi-site dataset with an existing model.

one_line: Models trained on physics-simulated images generalize across real sites better than single-site-real-trained models, because simulation training cannot learn real-site shortcuts.
problem: Synthetic medical data is evaluated on realism, but its structural advantage (absence of site-correlated shortcuts) as a generalization mechanism has not been isolated from its realism deficit.
core_hypothesis: Site shortcuts are a major component of cross-site failure, so simulation-trained models, which cannot acquire them, will lose less performance when moving across real sites than real-trained models lose, even if their absolute performance is lower, and the crossover point is measurable.
falsifiable_prediction: The cross-site degradation slope of simulation-trained models will be significantly flatter than that of single-site-real-trained models, and mixing small real data into simulation training will steepen the slope again, tracing shortcut acquisition.
why_important: This reframes synthetic data from a data-quantity story to a shortcut-hygiene story, motivating simulation as a regularizer rather than a substitute.
why_possibly_novel: Measuring shortcut acquisition through degradation-slope changes as real data is titrated in is a dose-response design connecting synthetic training to robustness mechanistically.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on simulated data, single-site real data, and titrated mixtures; evaluate degradation slopes across several real sites.
main_risk: Available simulators may be too unrealistic for the trained models to reach comparable operating points.
default_community_belief: Synthetic data is valued for volume and realism; less-realistic data is assumed strictly worse.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The simulation-to-real gap itself may behave like the worst site shift, flattening nothing.
fastest_falsification: Degradation-slope comparison using one public simulator and one multi-site dataset.

one_line: Test-time adaptation improves average Dice while increasing undetected catastrophic failures, a safety inversion measurable as tail-risk versus mean trade-off.
problem: Test-time adaptation (TTA) methods are evaluated on mean improvements under shift; their effect on the tail of the error distribution and on failure detectability is largely unreported.
core_hypothesis: TTA objectives (entropy minimization and variants) make outputs confident and self-consistent regardless of correctness, so adapted models convert detectable low-confidence failures into undetectable high-confidence failures, increasing clinical tail risk even as means improve.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing pre- and post-TTA on shifted data, the rate of high-confidence large errors will increase, failure-detection AUROC using confidence will drop substantially, and the worst-percentile Dice will not improve even when the mean does.
why_important: If TTA trades detectability for average gains, it is unsafe for autonomous clinical use despite favorable headline metrics, which changes how the field should evaluate it.
why_possibly_novel: The detectability-versus-mean trade-off framing evaluates TTA on failure-management grounds rather than accuracy grounds.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply one standard TTA method under controlled shift, measure mean Dice, tail Dice, and confidence-based failure-detection AUROC before and after.
main_risk: Findings may vary across TTA families; entropy-based conclusions may not indict augmentation-consistency methods.
default_community_belief: TTA is presented as a safe, free robustness gain under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some TTA variants may genuinely fix representations, improving both mean and tail together.
fastest_falsification: Tail and AUROC analysis of one TTA method on one shifted dataset.

one_line: Small-lesion recall versus size follows a sigmoid whose midpoint is set by the tokenization grid, not by data volume, so scaling data cannot move it but changing patch size can.
problem: Small-structure failure is universally observed but its governing variable (data, capacity, resolution, tokenization) is not isolated, leaving mitigation strategies unguided.
core_hypothesis: For transformer-based dense predictors, per-lesion recall as a function of lesion diameter is a sigmoid whose midpoint tracks the token patch size in physical units; interventions on data volume shift the curve's slope slightly but not its midpoint, while patch-size changes shift the midpoint proportionally.
falsifiable_prediction: Across models differing only in patch size, recall-curve midpoints will scale linearly with patch size; across models differing only in training-set size, midpoints will be statistically indistinguishable.
why_important: A tokenization-determined floor means the field's default remedy (more data) is provably ineffective for the small-lesion regime, redirecting effort to architecture.
why_possibly_novel: Separating data-scaling from tokenization effects on the recall curve with controlled interventions turns an anecdote into a quantitative law with design implications.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models at two patch sizes and two data scales on one lesion dataset, fit recall sigmoids, compare midpoints.
main_risk: Convolutional decoders on top of transformers may blur the tokenization signature.
default_community_belief: Small-lesion performance is expected to improve steadily with more training data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sub-token information flows through overlapping convolutions and positional interpolation may decouple the midpoint from patch size.
fastest_falsification: Midpoint comparison between two existing checkpoints of the same family with different patch sizes.

one_line: Pretraining-scale gains vanish below a structure-size threshold: scaling curves for medical transfer flatten to zero slope for structures smaller than the effective receptive resolution.
problem: Scaling laws for medical transfer are reported as aggregate curves; whether scale benefits are uniform across structure sizes determines who benefits from bigger models.
core_hypothesis: Pretraining scale improves representation quality for patterns above the model's effective resolution but cannot create sub-resolution sensitivity, so per-structure transfer gains versus pretraining scale will show positive slopes above a size threshold and flat slopes below it, with the threshold matching effective receptive resolution measured independently.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-structure gains on log pretraining scale, slope will be near zero for below-threshold structures across model families, and the threshold estimated from scaling data will agree with independently measured effective resolution.
why_important: This defines which clinical problems can ride the scaling wave and which need dedicated architectural solutions, informing investment decisions across the field.
why_possibly_novel: Size-stratified scaling analysis with an independently measured resolution threshold is a sharper decomposition than aggregate scaling curves.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a checkpoint ladder of one family on a size-diverse medical benchmark, fit size-stratified scaling slopes.
main_risk: Public checkpoint ladders confound scale with data and recipe changes.
default_community_belief: Scale is assumed to lift all tasks, with small structures benefiting from better features like everything else.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Larger models often have finer effective resolution through learned upsampling, coupling scale to the threshold itself.
fastest_falsification: Size-stratified evaluation of an existing checkpoint ladder on one dataset.

one_line: Texture-versus-shape reliance of foundation models inverts with structure scale in medical images: texture drives large-structure success but is unavailable at small scales, explaining the small-structure cliff.
problem: Texture-bias findings from natural images have not been decomposed by target scale in medical dense prediction, where small targets may not contain enough pixels to express texture at all.
core_hypothesis: For large structures, texture cues dominate and models are robust to shape perturbations; below a scale threshold the texture channel carries no information, and models fail because their shape pathway is comparatively undertrained, predicting that shape-biased training helps small structures specifically.
falsifiable_prediction: Texture-scrambling perturbations will degrade large-structure segmentation more than small-structure segmentation; shape-bias-inducing training will improve small-structure recall while leaving large structures unchanged or slightly worse.
why_important: A scale-dependent cue account provides a mechanism for the small-structure cliff and a targeted intervention (shape-pathway training) rather than generic scaling.
why_possibly_novel: Scale-conditional cue-reliance analysis in dense medical prediction connects the texture-bias literature to a concrete clinical failure mode.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply texture-scrambling and shape-perturbation tests stratified by structure size on one dataset; then train one shape-biased model and compare size-stratified gains.
main_risk: Perturbation methods for texture and shape are imperfectly orthogonal.
default_community_belief: Texture bias is treated as a global model property, not a scale-dependent one.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Small-structure detection may rely on context cues rather than either texture or shape of the target itself.
fastest_falsification: Size-stratified texture-scrambling sensitivity analysis, inference only.

one_line: Below a measurable size threshold, detect-then-segment pipelines beat end-to-end dense prediction, and the threshold is predictable from the dense model's recall curve, unifying two architecture camps.
problem: Detection-first and dense-prediction-first approaches for small lesions coexist without an account of when each wins, leading to inconsistent architecture choices.
core_hypothesis: Dense prediction loses small objects at the encoding stage while detectors allocate resolution adaptively, so a size threshold exists below which detection-plus-local-segmentation dominates; the threshold coincides with the dense model's recall-sigmoid midpoint, making it predictable without running the detector.
falsifiable_prediction: Across lesion sizes, the performance crossover between the two pipelines will occur within a small margin of the dense model's independently fitted recall midpoint, and this coincidence will replicate on a second dataset and model pair.
why_important: A predictable crossover converts architecture selection into a measurement, and clarifies that hybrid pipelines are not redundant engineering but principled responses to an encoding limit.
why_possibly_novel: Linking the crossover point to an independently measurable statistic of one pipeline gives the claim predictive force beyond a benchmark comparison.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit the dense recall sigmoid, run both pipelines size-stratified on one dataset, locate the crossover, replicate once.
main_risk: Crossover may be blurred by detector false positives complicating the comparison metric.
default_community_belief: End-to-end dense models are assumed to subsume detection pipelines given enough data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern dense models with deep supervision at multiple scales may have no meaningful encoding loss down to voxel scale.
fastest_falsification: Size-stratified comparison of one public detector pipeline and one dense model on one dataset.

one_line: Overlap-based losses impose a mathematical gradient ceiling on small structures, and gradient-contribution accounting predicts which structures cannot improve regardless of training length.
problem: Dice-family losses weight structures by size in their gradient contributions; the quantitative consequence, which structures are effectively untrained, has not been turned into a predictive audit.
core_hypothesis: Per-structure gradient mass during training predicts final per-structure performance rank, and structures below a gradient-mass threshold show no learning-curve progress; reweighting gradient mass, without any data or architecture change, moves exactly those structures, validating the accounting.
falsifiable_prediction: Logged per-structure gradient contributions will predict which structures plateau early; targeted loss reweighting will improve plateaued structures with minimal effect on others, matching the accounting's predictions quantitatively.
why_important: A gradient-accounting audit run early in training could predict and prevent wasted compute on structures the loss cannot learn, a practical training-diagnostics tool.
why_possibly_novel: Using gradient-mass accounting as a predictive per-structure diagnostic, validated by targeted intervention, goes beyond known qualitative loss-imbalance arguments.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument gradient contributions per structure in one training run, predict plateaus, verify with a reweighted second run.
main_risk: Gradient mass may interact with feature sharing across structures, blurring per-structure attribution.
default_community_belief: Loss imbalance is known qualitatively; training length and data are assumed to eventually lift all structures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared representations may let large-structure gradients improve small-structure features indirectly, breaking the accounting.
fastest_falsification: Correlation of logged gradient mass with per-structure learning curves in a single existing run.

one_line: Rare-but-large and common-but-small structures fail through different mechanisms (representation scarcity versus resolution), demonstrable by opposite responses to resampling and data-weighting interventions.
problem: Class imbalance and instance size are conflated in medical benchmarks: rare structures are often also small, so failure attributions are ambiguous and mitigations are misassigned.
core_hypothesis: Failure on rare-large structures is representational (fixed by data reweighting, unaffected by resolution changes), while failure on common-small structures is resolution-bound (fixed by resolution or tokenization changes, unaffected by reweighting); a two-by-two intervention will show this double dissociation.
falsifiable_prediction: Data reweighting will improve rare-large structures but not common-small ones; resolution increase will do the reverse; the interaction effect will be significant and replicate across two datasets.
why_important: A validated double dissociation gives practitioners a decision rule mapping observed failures to the correct (and cheaper) mitigation.
why_possibly_novel: The explicit two-mechanism theory with a crossed intervention design disentangles factors that ablation studies typically vary together.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Crossed reweighting-by-resolution training on one dataset with both structure types, interaction analysis.
main_risk: Few datasets contain clean examples of both structure classes with enough support.
default_community_belief: Rarity and smallness are lumped as the long tail, treated with the same oversampling remedies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both failure types may share a common cause (feature scarcity) responding to both interventions equally.
fastest_falsification: Reweighting-only arm on one dataset checking for the predicted selective improvement.

one_line: Super-resolution preprocessing improves small-structure recall only when the SR model is trained on matched modality physics; mismatched SR increases confident false positives, a net clinical harm.
problem: Off-the-shelf super-resolution is increasingly inserted before segmentation to rescue small structures, but its hallucination behavior under modality mismatch and its downstream effect on dense prediction are unaudited.
core_hypothesis: SR models hallucinate texture consistent with their training distribution; matched-physics SR adds true detail statistics while mismatched SR adds plausible-but-wrong detail that segmentation models trust, so downstream recall gains from matched SR coexist with false-positive inflation from mismatched SR.
falsifiable_prediction: In a matched-versus-mismatched SR comparison, small-structure recall will improve in both arms but false-positive rate will rise significantly only in the mismatched arm, and false positives will co-localize with SR-hallucinated texture measurable against ground-truth high-resolution data.
why_important: SR-plus-segmentation stacks are entering practice on recall arguments alone; the false-positive accounting determines actual clinical value.
why_possibly_novel: Auditing the SR-segmentation interaction with hallucination co-localization analysis treats the pipeline, not the components, as the unit of evaluation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Downsample high-resolution labeled data, apply matched and mismatched SR, run one segmentation model, compare recall and false-positive co-localization.
main_risk: Conclusions may depend on SR architecture family; two SR families should be included.
default_community_belief: SR preprocessing is assumed beneficial or neutral for downstream analysis if images look sharper.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation models may be insensitive to hallucinated texture, keying on geometry that SR reconstructs correctly in both arms.
fastest_falsification: False-positive co-localization analysis on one mismatched-SR arm with existing models.

one_line: The attention mass a transformer allocates to a structure predicts its segmentation quality, giving a training-free per-case small-structure reliability signal.
problem: There is no cheap per-case signal for whether a small structure was actually processed by the network or lost at encoding; attention maps might provide one but their predictive validity is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: Aggregate attention mass received by tokens overlapping a candidate structure region is causally upstream of segmentation quality there, so attention mass will predict per-structure Dice within-case and across cases, and attention-steering interventions will move quality in the predicted direction.
falsifiable_prediction: Attention mass will correlate strongly with per-structure quality after controlling for size and contrast, and inference-time attention boosting on under-attended regions will improve their segmentation at quantifiable cost elsewhere.
why_important: A validated attention-based reliability signal enables selective human review and targeted reprocessing for small structures without labels or ensembles.
why_possibly_novel: Testing the causal (steering) direction, not just correlation, distinguishes this from descriptive attention-visualization work.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract attention mass per structure on one dataset, regression against quality with covariate control, then a steering intervention on the low-attention stratum.
main_risk: Attention is an imperfect proxy for information flow, and steering may act through unrelated mechanisms.
default_community_belief: Attention maps are viewed as unreliable explanations, not as quantitatively predictive reliability signals.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Value-pathway information may bypass attention weights, making mass uninformative about processing quality.
fastest_falsification: Attention-mass-versus-quality regression on existing model outputs.

one_line: A substantial fraction of reported small-structure error is annotation jitter, measurable by multi-rater re-annotation, meaning true model error on small structures is systematically overestimated.
problem: Small-structure metrics are extremely sensitive to boundary placement, so rater jitter contributes disproportionately to measured error, yet benchmarks report it all as model error.
core_hypothesis: The rater-jitter share of measured small-structure error grows as structure size shrinks, and correcting for it with a jitter-noise model will reorder model comparisons on small structures because different models sit differently relative to the noise floor.
falsifiable_prediction: Multi-rater re-annotation of a small-structure subset will show inter-rater variability accounting for a large, size-dependent share of measured model error, and noise-corrected metrics will change small-structure model rankings while leaving large-structure rankings intact.
why_important: If the community is benchmarking annotation noise at small scales, small-structure leaderboard progress claims are partly illusory and evaluation protocols need noise-corrected metrics.
why_possibly_novel: Propagating a measured annotation-noise model into metric correction and testing ranking stability is measurement-error methodology rarely applied to segmentation benchmarks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate a stratified small-structure sample with multiple raters, estimate the jitter noise model, recompute noise-corrected metrics for existing models.
main_risk: Multi-rater annotation cost limits sample size; power analysis must precede.
default_community_belief: Ground truth is treated as exact; all deviation is attributed to the model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For high-contrast small structures rater agreement may be excellent, leaving little error to reattribute.
fastest_falsification: Jitter estimation on a small re-annotated sample against existing model errors.

one_line: Calibration inverts with structure size: models are overconfident on small structures and underconfident on large ones, so size-conditional recalibration beats global temperature scaling.
problem: Calibration is assessed globally, but the mechanisms of confidence formation (boundary fraction, context support) vary systematically with structure size, suggesting size-dependent miscalibration patterns.
core_hypothesis: Small structures have high boundary-to-interior ratios and weak context support, producing inflated confidence from interior-dominated calibration training, while large structures accumulate conservative boundary uncertainty over long perimeters; calibration curves stratified by size will show opposite-sign deviations.
falsifiable_prediction: Size-stratified reliability diagrams will show overconfidence for the smallest stratum and underconfidence for the largest, a pattern consistent across datasets, and size-conditional temperature scaling will significantly beat global scaling on small-structure calibration error.
why_important: Confidence-based review triage currently treats all structures alike; size-conditional recalibration is a cheap fix with direct safety consequences for small-lesion review.
why_possibly_novel: Identifying a systematic sign inversion with a mechanistic account, rather than reporting average calibration error, gives an actionable structural result.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Size-stratified reliability analysis of one model on two datasets, then paired comparison of global versus size-conditional temperature scaling.
main_risk: The sign pattern may be architecture-dependent, requiring multiple model families for a general claim.
default_community_belief: Miscalibration is treated as a global scalar fixable by one temperature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two proposed mechanisms may cancel or interact differently, producing no clean size trend.
fastest_falsification: Size-stratified reliability diagram on existing predictions of one dataset.

one_line: Hard-example mining collapses onto a few structure types and starves the rest, so mining improves targeted structures while measurably degrading unmined small structures, a hidden redistribution.
problem: Online hard-example mining is standard in medical training, but which examples it actually selects over training, and what the selection concentration does to non-selected structures, is rarely audited.
core_hypothesis: Mining criteria concentrate on a small set of persistently hard structure types, redirecting capacity toward them; unmined structures lose performance relative to uniform training, so mining is a reallocation whose winners and losers are predictable from the mining-selection log.
falsifiable_prediction: Selection logs will show heavy concentration (a small type share dominating mined batches); per-structure comparison against uniform-sampling baselines will show gains for dominant mined types and losses for rarely mined small structures, with the gain-loss pattern predictable from selection shares.
why_important: If mining silently taxes unmined anatomy, standard training recipes carry an undisclosed clinical prioritization that should be surfaced and controlled.
why_possibly_novel: Auditing mining as a capacity-allocation mechanism with predictive gain-loss accounting reframes a routine trick as a policy choice.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log mining selections in one standard training run, train a uniform-sampling control, compare per-structure outcomes against selection shares.
main_risk: Effects may be small at large model capacity where allocation trade-offs soften.
default_community_belief: Mining is assumed to help hard cases without hurting anything else.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared features may propagate mining gains broadly, yielding no measurable losers.
fastest_falsification: Selection-log concentration analysis on an existing training run.

one_line: Final-resolution token budget, not curriculum order, determines small-structure performance: coarse-to-fine training schedules are interchangeable at matched final budgets.
problem: Progressive-resolution curricula are credited with small-structure gains, but budget and schedule are confounded in existing reports, leaving the causal factor unidentified.
core_hypothesis: Small-structure capability is set by the token budget at the final training resolution; any schedule reaching the same final budget for sufficient steps converges to equivalent small-structure performance, so curriculum design is a compute-efficiency question, not a capability question.
falsifiable_prediction: Compute-matched runs with different schedules but identical final-resolution exposure will show statistically indistinguishable small-structure metrics, while runs differing in final budget will separate cleanly regardless of schedule.
why_important: Disentangling schedule from budget prevents the field from optimizing the wrong variable and simplifies training-recipe search to a single number.
why_possibly_novel: The equivalence claim (schedules interchangeable at matched budgets) is a strong null-structure hypothesis that existing curriculum papers do not test.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three schedules at matched final budget plus one budget-varied arm on one dataset, small-structure metric comparison with seed replication.
main_risk: Optimization dynamics may genuinely interact with schedule at the edge of stability, breaking equivalence for reasons unrelated to the hypothesis.
default_community_belief: Curriculum order itself is believed to build better small-structure features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Early low-resolution phases may shape features irreversibly, making order matter even at matched final budgets.
fastest_falsification: Two-schedule matched-budget comparison on one dataset.

one_line: Voxelwise model uncertainty and inter-rater uncertainty are weakly correlated once distance-to-boundary is controlled, refuting the common claim that model uncertainty captures ambiguity.
problem: Papers routinely assert that predicted uncertainty maps reflect clinical ambiguity, but the shared correlation with boundary proximity may explain the entire apparent agreement.
core_hypothesis: Both model uncertainty and rater disagreement peak near boundaries for trivial geometric reasons; after conditioning on distance-to-boundary, the residual correlation between them is near zero, meaning models capture where boundaries are, not which boundaries are ambiguous.
falsifiable_prediction: Partial correlation between model uncertainty and rater disagreement given boundary distance will be dramatically lower than the raw correlation, approaching zero for most structures, across multiple uncertainty methods.
why_important: If uncertainty maps only re-encode boundary geometry, their clinical value proposition (flagging genuinely ambiguous regions) collapses, redirecting research toward ambiguity-specific supervision.
why_possibly_novel: The boundary-distance-conditioned analysis targets a confound that raw correlation studies in the literature do not remove.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-rater dataset, compute raw and boundary-conditioned correlations between rater variance and uncertainty from three methods (entropy, ensemble, dropout).
main_risk: Boundary distance may be too coarse a confound model; geometry may need richer parameterization.
default_community_belief: Predicted uncertainty is presented as a proxy for annotation ambiguity, supported by raw correlation numbers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ensembles may genuinely track intensity-driven ambiguity beyond geometry, retaining solid partial correlation.
fastest_falsification: Partial-correlation analysis on existing predictions and multi-rater labels, no training.

one_line: Ensemble disagreement in medical dense prediction concentrates where aleatoric ambiguity lives, so the standard epistemic-aleatoric decomposition mislabels uncertainty sources.
problem: The standard decomposition treats ensemble spread as epistemic (reducible) uncertainty, but in ambiguous medical regions all ensemble members face the same underdetermined target, which may drive spread that is actually aleatoric in origin.
core_hypothesis: In ambiguity zones, training labels are effectively stochastic, so independently trained members learn different arbitrary commitments; ensemble spread there reflects label ambiguity (aleatoric) and will not shrink with more training data, violating the decomposition's core reducibility promise.
falsifiable_prediction: Scaling training data will shrink ensemble spread in unambiguous regions but not in high-rater-disagreement regions, whereas adding raters (better label distributions) will shrink modeled aleatoric terms but leave the decomposition misattributing zone-specific spread.
why_important: Uncertainty-based clinical triage relies on the reducible-versus-irreducible distinction; a systematic misattribution breaks downstream logic like targeted data collection.
why_possibly_novel: The data-scaling versus rater-scaling intervention pair directly tests reducibility claims rather than assuming them from the mathematical form.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train ensembles at multiple data scales on a multi-rater dataset, track spread by rater-disagreement zone, compare against decomposition predictions.
main_risk: Requires several ensemble trainings; compute-heavy though conceptually simple.
default_community_belief: Ensemble spread is treated as epistemic uncertainty that more data reduces.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With enough data all members may converge to the majority label mode even in ambiguous zones, restoring the decomposition's validity.
fastest_falsification: Two-data-scale ensemble comparison restricted to high-disagreement zones.

one_line: Conformal mask pairs achieve marginal coverage but fail per-structure and per-patient conditional coverage in predictable directions, quantifying the gap between statistical and clinical validity.
problem: Conformal prediction offers distribution-free coverage for segmentation via inner-outer mask pairs, but marginal guarantees may hide systematic under-coverage for exactly the difficult patients and structures.
core_hypothesis: Nonconformity scores are heteroscedastic across structures and patient difficulty, so marginal coverage is achieved by over-covering easy cases and under-covering hard ones; the under-coverage direction is predictable from case difficulty proxies, making the guarantee clinically misleading in a diagnosable way.
falsifiable_prediction: Empirical conditional coverage will fall significantly below nominal for the hardest difficulty quartile and smallest structures, with over-coverage on easy quartiles, and difficulty-stratified conformal calibration will restore conditional coverage at the cost of wider easy-case bands.
why_important: Conformal methods are being proposed for regulatory-grade uncertainty claims; documenting where the guarantee fails conditionally is essential before such claims reach practice.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic conditional-coverage audit for dense medical prediction with difficulty-predictable failure directions goes beyond demonstrating marginal validity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement inner-outer conformal masks on one dataset, audit coverage stratified by structure, size, and difficulty proxy, test stratified recalibration.
main_risk: Small strata inflate coverage-estimate variance; dataset must be large enough per stratum.
default_community_belief: Distribution-free coverage is presented as solving uncertainty quantification for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Well-chosen nonconformity scores may be nearly homoscedastic, keeping conditional coverage acceptable.
fastest_falsification: Stratified coverage audit of a basic conformal implementation on one dataset.

one_line: Catastrophic segmentation failures are better detected by mask-shape anomaly statistics than by model confidence, because confidence fails silently while shape cannot lie.
problem: Clinical deployment needs automatic detection of catastrophic outputs (empty masks, wrong organ, fragment explosions), and the default detector, model confidence, may itself fail under the same conditions that cause the catastrophe.
core_hypothesis: Failure causes (shift, artifacts) corrupt confidence and prediction jointly, but output-mask geometry deviates from anatomical shape statistics in ways detectable by a label-free shape model, so shape-based detection will dominate confidence-based detection specifically on the catastrophic subset.
falsifiable_prediction: On induced-failure test sets, detection AUROC for catastrophic failures will be substantially higher for shape-statistic anomaly scores than for confidence-based scores, and combining them will add little over shape alone for the catastrophic subset.
why_important: Catastrophic-failure gating is the minimum safety requirement for autonomous use; identifying which signal family actually works there is directly deployable knowledge.
why_possibly_novel: The joint-corruption argument for why confidence must fail on catastrophes, tested against an independent output-side signal, is a structured comparison rather than another QC heuristic.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Induce failures via shift and corruption on one dataset, build a simple shape-statistics anomaly detector from training masks, compare detection AUROC against confidence baselines.
main_risk: Shape detectors may miss anatomically plausible but wrongly located masks, a specific catastrophe subtype.
default_community_belief: Low confidence is assumed to accompany bad outputs enough to serve as the failure alarm.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern well-calibrated models may retain informative confidence even under the failure-inducing conditions tested.
fastest_falsification: AUROC comparison of the two detector families on one induced-failure suite.

one_line: Uncertainty of promptable models is prompt-conditional, and marginalizing over plausible prompts yields better-calibrated uncertainty than any single-prompt estimate, at quantifiable compute cost.
problem: Promptable segmentation produces uncertainty conditioned on one arbitrary prompt, conflating model uncertainty with prompt choice; the calibration cost of this conditioning is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: A significant share of predictive uncertainty lives in the prompt dimension: single-prompt uncertainty underestimates total uncertainty in ambiguous regions and overestimates it where the prompt was unluckily placed, so prompt-marginalized uncertainty will dominate in calibration and failure-prediction metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: Prompt-marginalized uncertainty (averaging over a plausible prompt distribution) will improve calibration error and error-prediction AUROC over single-prompt uncertainty by a margin exceeding ensemble-over-seeds baselines at matched compute.
why_important: This defines the correct uncertainty object for interactive clinical tools and shows that ignoring prompt variance produces unsafe confidence estimates.
why_possibly_novel: Treating the prompt as a latent variable to marginalize, and benchmarking against compute-matched ensembles, formalizes an overlooked uncertainty source unique to promptable architectures.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare calibration and failure-prediction metrics for single-prompt, prompt-marginalized, and seed-ensemble uncertainty on one dataset at matched inference budgets.
main_risk: The plausible-prompt distribution is a design choice that influences results and must be justified.
default_community_belief: Uncertainty is treated as a property of the model given an input, with the prompt regarded as fixed context rather than a variance source.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt encoders may be so robust that prompt variance is negligible next to model variance.
fastest_falsification: Variance decomposition of predictions over prompts versus over seeds on a few hundred cases.

one_line: Temperature scaling fitted on one anatomy does not transfer to any other anatomy, revealing that dense-prediction miscalibration is structure-specific rather than model-global.
problem: Post-hoc calibration for segmentation is usually fitted globally or on a convenience structure, assuming miscalibration is a shared scalar property of the model.
core_hypothesis: Miscalibration arises from structure-specific factors (boundary fraction, contrast regime, label noise), so a temperature fitted on one organ will be systematically wrong for others, and the fitted-temperature landscape across organs will be wide, structured, and predictable from those factors.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-structure transfer of fitted temperatures will often be worse than no calibration at all; per-structure optimal temperatures will span a wide range and regress well on boundary fraction and contrast statistics.
why_important: Global calibration is standard practice before clinical confidence use; demonstrating negative transfer would show current practice can actively harm calibration for unmonitored structures.
why_possibly_novel: Mapping and explaining the per-structure temperature landscape, including the negative-transfer regime, treats calibration as a structured phenomenon rather than a scalar fix.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit per-structure and global temperatures on a multi-organ dataset, evaluate the full transfer matrix, regress optimal temperatures on structure statistics.
main_risk: Per-structure calibration sets may be small, making fitted temperatures noisy.
default_community_belief: One temperature per model is considered adequate for segmentation confidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared backbone logit statistics may dominate, keeping optimal temperatures in a narrow transferable band.
fastest_falsification: Temperature transfer matrix on existing predictions of one multi-organ dataset.

one_line: Feature-space distance to the pretraining manifold predicts dense-prediction error better than output-level uncertainty, unifying OOD detection and error estimation for medical foundation models.
problem: Output uncertainty and OOD scores are treated as separate tools; for foundation models the feature-manifold geometry may subsume both for predicting where dense predictions fail.
core_hypothesis: Errors of frozen-backbone medical segmentation are dominated by feature-space extrapolation, so patchwise distance-to-manifold scores (computed from pretraining feature statistics) will outperform output entropy and match ensembles in voxel-level error prediction, especially under distribution shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Across in-distribution and shifted test sets, patchwise manifold-distance scores will achieve higher error-prediction AUROC than output entropy, with the advantage growing with shift magnitude, and will localize error regions that entropy misses entirely.
why_important: A backbone-intrinsic error predictor requires no ensembles or labels and would give foundation-model pipelines a native reliability layer.
why_possibly_novel: Voxel-level error prediction from pretraining-manifold geometry, benchmarked against uncertainty methods under controlled shift, connects representation geometry to dense reliability in a directly testable way.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate feature-density models on pretraining-like data, compute patchwise distances on test sets with known errors, compare error-prediction metrics against entropy and a small ensemble.
main_risk: Density estimation in high-dimensional feature spaces is fragile and choices may drive conclusions.
default_community_belief: Output-level uncertainty is the default error proxy; OOD scoring is treated as a separate input-level gate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuned heads may correct extrapolated features, decoupling manifold distance from realized error.
fastest_falsification: AUROC comparison of manifold distance versus entropy on one shifted dataset.

one_line: Voxel-level selective prediction fails clinically because errors are spatially clustered: rejecting the most-uncertain voxels removes scattered noise while leaving coherent wrong regions intact.
problem: Selective prediction (abstaining on uncertain voxels) is proposed for safety, but its voxel-level formulation ignores that clinically dangerous errors are contiguous regions, not salt-and-pepper noise.
core_hypothesis: Uncertainty ranks scattered boundary voxels above interior voxels of coherent error regions, so at practical rejection budgets voxel-level abstention removes mostly harmless boundary noise; region-level abstention (rejecting connected components by aggregate scores) will dominate at equal budget on clinically weighted metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched rejection budgets, voxel-level selection will reduce clinically weighted error far less than region-level selection, and the residual accepted error after voxel-level selection will remain dominated by large coherent components.
why_important: This redirects the selective-prediction literature toward spatially coherent abstention units, which is what clinical review workflows actually need.
why_possibly_novel: The spatial-clustering critique of voxelwise abstention, with a region-unit alternative evaluated on clinically weighted metrics, targets the formulation rather than the uncertainty estimator.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both abstention schemes over a budget sweep on one dataset, compare residual clinically weighted error and component-size distribution of accepted errors.
main_risk: Defining clinically weighted error requires justified weighting; sensitivity analysis over weightings is needed.
default_community_belief: Higher voxel uncertainty is assumed to identify the voxels most worth abstaining on.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Coherent error regions may carry elevated aggregate uncertainty, letting voxel-level selection find them after all.
fastest_falsification: Component-size analysis of errors surviving voxel-level rejection on existing predictions.

one_line: Models calibrated at coarse label granularity are systematically miscalibrated at fine granularity, so hierarchy-aware calibration is necessary for subregion-level clinical use.
problem: Medical labels are hierarchical (organ, subregion, lesion compartment), and calibration is typically performed and verified at one level, assuming validity propagates down the hierarchy.
core_hypothesis: Aggregating well-calibrated fine-level probabilities does not require fine-level calibration, and conversely coarse calibration constrains fine calibration only weakly, so coarse-calibrated models will show large fine-level calibration errors with a bias direction determined by subregion prevalence within the parent structure.
falsifiable_prediction: Calibration error measured at subregion level will be several times the parent-level error for coarse-calibrated models, with overconfidence concentrated in low-prevalence subregions, and hierarchical recalibration will fix fine level without damaging coarse level.
why_important: Clinical decisions increasingly use subregion quantification (e.g., compartment volumes); level-blind calibration certification would approve models that are unreliable exactly where used.
why_possibly_novel: Formalizing and measuring calibration non-propagation across label hierarchies raises an evaluation requirement current practice does not include.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Calibrate at parent level on a hierarchically labeled dataset, audit child-level calibration, apply hierarchical recalibration, compare both levels.
main_risk: Requires datasets with reliable nested labels, which narrows options.
default_community_belief: Calibration verified at the reported level is assumed sufficient for derived quantities at other levels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared logit geometry across levels may make calibration approximately propagate in practice.
fastest_falsification: Child-level calibration audit of a parent-calibrated model on one nested-label dataset.

one_line: Diffusion-based mask samplers reproduce the modes of inter-rater contour distributions but with systematically wrong mode weights, making them qualitatively right and quantitatively unusable.
problem: Generative mask samplers are promoted as capturing multimodal ambiguity, but evaluation focuses on sample diversity, not on whether the sampled distribution matches the true rater distribution in mode frequencies.
core_hypothesis: Training dynamics of generative segmentation over-represent high-data-density modes and distort tail-mode frequencies, so sampled mode proportions will deviate substantially from rater proportions even when every rater mode appears among samples, and the deviation will grow for minority contour conventions.
falsifiable_prediction: Matching samples to rater modes on multi-rater data, mode coverage will be high but mode-frequency divergence will be large, with minority modes under-sampled by measurable factors, and reweighting-based fixes will improve frequency match without hurting coverage.
why_important: Downstream uses (risk-weighted planning, expected-volume estimation) need correct mode weights, not just mode existence; wrong weights bias every derived quantity.
why_possibly_novel: Shifting the evaluation criterion from diversity or coverage to distributional frequency match against real rater distributions imposes the standard the application actually requires.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or use one generative mask sampler on a multi-rater dataset, cluster samples against rater modes, quantify frequency divergence and test a reweighting correction.
main_risk: Few datasets have enough raters to estimate true mode frequencies reliably.
default_community_belief: Generating diverse plausible masks is treated as solving the ambiguity-representation problem.
